content.code:
# .gitlab-ci.yml - Advanced Configuration

# Define stages
stages:
  - lint
  - test
  - build
  - security
  - package
  - review
  - staging
  - production
  - performance

# Global variables
variables:
  NODE_VERSION: '18'
  DOCKER_DRIVER: overlay2
  DOCKER_TLS_CERTDIR: ''
  CACHE_FALLBACK_KEY: main
  
# Cache configuration
cache:
  key:
    files:
      - package-lock.json
  paths:
    - node_modules/
    - .npm/
  policy: pull-push

# Default configuration for all jobs
default:
  image: node:${NODE_VERSION}
  before_script:
    - npm ci --cache .npm --prefer-offline
  interruptible: true
  timeout: 30m

# Include external templates
include:
  - template: Security/SAST.gitlab-ci.yml
  - template: Security/Dependency-Scanning.gitlab-ci.yml
  - template: Security/Secret-Detection.gitlab-ci.yml
  - project: 'my-group/shared-pipelines'
    file: '/deploy-templates.yml'
    ref: v1.2.3

# Lint job
lint:
  stage: lint
  script:
    - npm run lint
    - npm run format:check
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == 'merge_request_event'
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH

# Parallel test matrix
test:
  stage: test
  parallel:
    matrix:
      - TEST_SUITE: [unit, integration, e2e]
        NODE_VERSION: [16, 18, 20]
  script:
    - npm run test:${TEST_SUITE}
  artifacts:
    when: always
    reports:
      junit: junit.xml
      coverage_report:
        coverage_format: cobertura
        path: coverage/cobertura-coverage.xml
    paths:
      - coverage/
      - cypress/screenshots/
    expire_in: 1 week

# Build job with caching
build:
  stage: build
  script:
    - npm run build
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - dist/
    expire_in: 1 hour
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH

# Security scanning
security:
  stage: security
  script:
    - npm audit --production
    - snyk test
  allow_failure: true
  artifacts:
    reports:
      security: gl-security-report.json

# Package Docker image
package:
  stage: package
  image: docker:latest
  services:
    - docker:dind
  script:
    - docker build -t $CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHA .
    - docker tag $CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHA $CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:latest
    - docker login -u $CI_REGISTRY_USER -p $CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD $CI_REGISTRY
    - docker push $CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHA
    - docker push $CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:latest
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
      exists:
        - Dockerfile

# Review app - temporary environment for MRs
review:
  stage: review
  image: alpine:latest
  script:
    - apk add --no-cache curl
    - curl -X POST https://api.vercel.com/deploy
  environment:
    name: review/$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG
    url: https://review-$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG.example.com
    on_stop: stop_review
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == 'merge_request_event'

stop_review:
  stage: review
  image: alpine:latest
  script:
    - apk add --no-cache curl
    - curl -X DELETE https://api.vercel.com/deploy
  environment:
    name: review/$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG
    action: stop
  rules:
    - if: $CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == 'merge_request_event'
      when: manual

# Deploy to staging
deploy-staging:
  stage: staging
  image: alpine:latest
  script:
    - chmod +x deploy.sh
    - ./deploy.sh staging
  environment:
    name: staging
    url: https://staging.example.com
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH

# Performance testing
performance:
  stage: performance
  image: grafana/k6
  script:
    - k6 run performance-tests.js
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - performance-report.html
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
      changes:
        - performance-tests.js
        - src/**/*.js

# Deploy to production (manual gate)
deploy-production:
  stage: production
  image: alpine:latest
  script:
    - ./deploy.sh production
  environment:
    name: production
    url: https://example.com
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_TAG
  when: manual
  needs:
    - job: performance
      optional: true

# Post-deployment validation
post-deploy:
  stage: production
  script:
    - npm run test:smoke -- --url=https://example.com
  needs:
    - deploy-production
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_TAG

# Notifications
slack-notify:
  stage: .post
  image: alpine:latest
  script:
    - apk add --no-cache curl
    - curl -X POST -H 'Content-type: application/json' --data '{"text":"Pipeline $CI_PIPELINE_STATUS for $CI_PROJECT_NAME"}' $SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_BRANCH == $CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_TAG
  when: always

content.title: GitHub Actions Deep Dive
content.explanation:
GitHub Actions integrates CI/CD directly into GitHub repositories. Workflows are defined in YAML and triggered by repository events (push, PR, release).

**Key Features:**
- **Event-Driven** – Trigger on any GitHub event (push, PR, issue comment, release)
- **Marketplace** – Thousands of pre-built actions for common tasks
- **Matrix Builds** – Test across multiple OSes, languages, and versions
- **Self-Hosted Runners** – Run actions on your own infrastructure
- **Environment Protection** – Manual approvals and environment variables
- **Secrets Management** – Encrypted secrets at organization and repository level
- **Artifacts** – Store and share build outputs
- **Packages** – Integrated container and package registry

**Architecture:**
- **Workflow** – YAML file defining automation
- **Job** – Collection of steps running on same runner
- **Step** – Individual task (run script or action)
- **Runner** – Server that executes jobs (GitHub-hosted or self-hosted)
- **Action** – Reusable unit of code (like a function)

**Runner Types:**
- **GitHub-hosted** – Ubuntu, Windows, macOS (free for public repos)
- **Self-hosted** – Run on your infrastructure (more control, free)
- **Larger Runners** – Premium runners with more CPU/RAM
- **GPU Runners** – For ML/AI workloads

content.caption: Advanced GitHub Actions Workflow
content.code:
name: Advanced CI/CD Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [main, develop]
    tags: ['v*']
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
  release:
    types: [published]
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      environment:
        description: 'Deployment environment'
        required: true
        default: 'staging'
        type: choice
        options:
          - staging
          - production

# Concurrency control
concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

# Environment variables
env:
  NODE_VERSION: '18'
  PNPM_VERSION: '8'
  REGISTRY: ghcr.io
  IMAGE_NAME: ${{ github.repository }}

jobs:
  # Security scan job
  security:
    name: Security Scan
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      security-events: write
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      
      - name: Initialize CodeQL
        uses: github/codeql-action/init@v2
        with:
          languages: javascript
      
      - name: Perform CodeQL Analysis
        uses: github/codeql-action/analyze@v2
      
      - name: Run Trivy vulnerability scanner
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
        with:
          scan-type: 'fs'
          scan-ref: '.'
          format: 'sarif'
          output: 'trivy-results.sarif'
      
      - name: Upload Trivy results to GitHub Security
        uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v2
        with:
          sarif_file: 'trivy-results.sarif'

  # Build and test matrix
  build:
    name: Build and Test
    needs: security
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, macos-latest]
        node-version: [16.x, 18.x, 20.x]
        include:
          - os: ubuntu-latest
            node-version: 18.x
            coverage: true
        exclude:
          - os: windows-latest
            node-version: 16.x
    
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      
      - name: Setup pnpm
        uses: pnpm/action-setup@v2
        with:
          version: ${{ env.PNPM_VERSION }}
      
      - name: Setup Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}
          cache: 'pnpm'
      
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: pnpm install
      
      - name: Lint
        run: pnpm lint
      
      - name: Type check
        run: pnpm type-check
      
      - name: Run tests
        run: pnpm test -- --coverage
      
      - name: Upload coverage to Codecov
        if: matrix.coverage
        uses: codecov/codecov-action@v3
        with:
          token: ${{ secrets.CODECOV_TOKEN }}
          files: ./coverage/lcov.info
          flags: unittests
      
      - name: Upload test results
        if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
        with:
          name: test-results-${{ matrix.os }}-${{ matrix.node-version }}
          path: |
            junit.xml
            coverage/

  # Build Docker image
  docker:
    name: Build Docker Image
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: github.event_name != 'pull_request'
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write
    
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      
      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v2
      
      - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
        uses: docker/login-action@v2
        with:
          registry: ${{ env.REGISTRY }}
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      
      - name: Extract metadata
        id: meta
        uses: docker/metadata-action@v4
        with:
          images: ${{ env.REGISTRY }}/${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}
          tags: |
            type=semver,pattern={{version}}
            type=semver,pattern={{major}}.{{minor}}
            type=sha,format=long
            type=ref,event=branch
            type=raw,value=latest,enable={{is_default_branch}}
      
      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v4
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }}
          labels: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.labels }}
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

  # Deploy to environments
  deploy:
    name: Deploy to ${{ inputs.environment || 'staging' }}
    needs: docker
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' || github.event_name == 'release'
    environment:
      name: ${{ github.event_name == 'release' && 'production' || 'staging' }}
      url: ${{ steps.deploy.outputs.url }}
    
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      
      - name: Configure AWS credentials
        uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v2
        if: env.ACTIONS_STEP_DEBUG != 'true'
        with:
          aws-access-key-id: ${{ secrets.AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID }}
          aws-secret-access-key: ${{ secrets.AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY }}
          aws-region: us-east-1
      
      - name: Deploy to ECS
        id: deploy
        run: |
          aws ecs update-service --cluster myapp --service ${{ env.ENVIRONMENT }} --force-new-deployment
          echo "url=https://${{ env.ENVIRONMENT }}.example.com" >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT
        env:
          ENVIRONMENT: ${{ github.event_name == 'release' && 'production' || 'staging' }}

  # Smoke tests
  smoke:
    name: Smoke Tests
    needs: deploy
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      
      - name: Run smoke tests
        run: |
          npx wait-on https://${{ needs.deploy.outputs.url }}
          npm run test:smoke -- --url=https://${{ needs.deploy.outputs.url }}

  # Performance tests
  performance:
    name: Performance Tests
    needs: deploy
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: github.event_name == 'release'
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      
      - name: Run k6 tests
        uses: grafana/k6-action@v0.3.0
        with:
          filename: performance-tests.js
          flags: --vus 10 --duration 30s

  # Notifications
  notify:
    name: Send Notifications
    needs: [build, security, smoke]
    if: always()
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Notify Slack
        uses: 8398a7/action-slack@v3
        with:
          status: ${{ job.status }}
          fields: repo,message,commit,author,action,workflow
        env:
          SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL: ${{ secrets.SLACK_WEBHOOK }}

content.title: 10.1 The Role of Testing in CI
Testing is the Heart of CI
content.explanation:
Testing is the heartbeat of Continuous Integration. Without automated tests, CI pipelines are just automated build systems—they confirm that code compiles, but not that it works correctly.

The combination of unit, integration, system, performance, and security testing ensures that every change is validated quickly and reliably. A CI pipeline without comprehensive testing provides false confidence and can actually accelerate the delivery of defective software.

The Test Pyramid in CI follows a layered structure:

Top Layer – End-to-End (E2E) Tests:
Few in number, slow to execute, and more brittle. These validate complete user journeys and should focus only on critical business paths.

Middle Layer – Integration Tests:
Moderate in number and execution speed. These verify interactions between components, services, databases, and APIs.

Base Layer – Unit Tests:
High in number, fast, and reliable. These test individual functions or classes in isolation and should form 70–80% of the total test suite.

A healthy CI pipeline relies heavily on fast unit tests, supported by targeted integration tests and a minimal set of E2E tests. This structure ensures rapid feedback while maintaining confidence in system stability.

content.title: 10.2 Types of Tests in CI Pipelines

items.definition: Validate individual functions, methods, or classes in isolation. Mock all dependencies. Should run in milliseconds. Tools: JUnit, NUnit, pytest, Jest, Mocha.

Verify that components work together correctly. May use real databases, file systems, or external services. Slower than unit tests but catch interface issues. Tools: TestContainers, SpringBootTest, Docker Compose.
Test a component in isolation with its dependencies stubbed. Broader than unit tests but narrower than integration tests. Tools: WireMock, MockServer.
Verify that service providers and consumers agree on API contracts. Essential for microservices. Tools: Pact, Spring Cloud Contract.
Test complete user journeys through the entire application stack. Slowest and most brittle. Focus on critical paths. Tools: Selenium, Cypress, Playwright, TestCafe.
Validate that the software meets business requirements. Often written in business-readable formats (Gherkin). Tools: Cucumber, SpecFlow, Behave.
Measure system speed, scalability, and resource usage under load. Run less frequently due to time/resource requirements. Tools: k6, JMeter, Gatling, Locust.
Identify vulnerabilities in code, dependencies, and configuration. Tools: SAST (SonarQube, CodeQL), DAST (OWASP ZAP), dependency scanning (Snyk, Dependabot).
Evaluate test quality by introducing small changes (mutations) to code and seeing if tests catch them. Tools: Stryker, PIT.
Quick sanity checks after deployment to verify basic functionality. Fast subset of E2E tests. Run after every deployment.
Ensure new changes haven't broken existing functionality. Often a combination of unit, integration, and E2E tests.
Detect unintended visual changes in UI. Compare screenshots against baselines. Tools: Percy, Applitools, Chromatic.

content.title: Optimizing Test Execution in CI
content.explanation:
As test suites grow, execution time becomes a critical concern. Slow tests delay feedback and reduce developer productivity. Here are strategies to keep tests fast while maintaining coverage:

**1. Test Parallelization**
Split tests across multiple machines or containers. Most CI tools support parallel test execution:
- GitHub Actions: `strategy.matrix`
- GitLab CI: `parallel` keyword
- Jenkins: Parallel stages
- CircleCI: Test splitting with `circleci tests split`

**2. Test Impact Analysis**
Run only tests that cover changed code. Tools like Bazel, Nx, and Turborepo analyze dependencies to determine which tests need to run.

**3. Test Sharding**
Divide tests into groups and run each group in parallel. Tools like Jest, pytest, and JUnit support sharding.

**4. Test Prioritization**
Run critical tests first (smoke tests, unit tests), then longer-running tests. Fail fast to save resources.

**5. Test Caching**
Cache test results to avoid re-running unchanged tests. Tools like Jest have built-in caching; CI systems can cache test outputs.

**6. Flaky Test Management**
Flaky tests (tests that sometimes pass, sometimes fail) undermine trust. Identify, quarantine, and fix them aggressively.

**7. Test Containerization**
Run tests in containers for consistent environments and easy parallelization.

**8. Database State Management**
Reset database state between tests. Use transactions, Docker snapshots, or tools like TestContainers.

content.title: Managing Test Data for Reliable Pipelines
content.explanation:
Reliable test data is essential for reproducible builds. In CI pipelines, teams need strategies to ensure tests run with consistent, predictable data.

**Challenges with Test Data in CI:**
- Databases start empty or with inconsistent state
- External APIs may be unavailable or rate-limited
- Sensitive production data cannot be used
- Tests may interfere with each other when run in parallel

**Test Data Strategies:**

1. **In-Memory Databases** – Use H2, SQLite, or other in-memory databases for fast, isolated tests.

2. **Database Snapshots** – Restore a known database state before tests. Tools like TestContainers, Docker, or Flyway can manage this.

3. **Transactional Tests** – Run each test in a transaction and roll back after completion.

4. **Factory/Builder Patterns** – Generate test data programmatically using factories (e.g., Factory Bot for Ruby, Factory Boy for Python).

5. **Seed Scripts** – Maintain scripts that populate databases with consistent seed data.

6. **Masked Production Data** – Use anonymized subsets of production data for realistic testing while protecting privacy.

7. **API Stubs/Mocks** – Use tools like WireMock, Mountebank, or MockServer to simulate external APIs.

8. **Service Virtualization** – Virtualize entire dependent services for integration testing.

9. **Parallel Test Isolation** – Use unique schemas or namespaces for parallel test runs to prevent interference.

content.title: Measuring Pipeline Health and Effectiveness
content.explanation:
Metrics ensure that CI pipelines deliver business value. Without measurement, you can't improve. Here are critical KPIs to track and optimize.

**Why Measure CI Metrics?**
- Identify bottlenecks and inefficiencies
- Track progress over time
- Justify investments in tooling and infrastructure
- Build a data-driven culture
- Alert when pipelines degrade

**Key Categories of CI Metrics:**
1. **Speed Metrics** – How fast is feedback?
2. **Reliability Metrics** – How trustworthy is the pipeline?
3. **Quality Metrics** – How effective is testing?
4. **Productivity Metrics** – How much value is delivered?
5. **Adoption Metrics** – How well is CI practiced?

content.title: Comprehensive CI Metrics Dashboard
rows: Percentage of builds that pass all stages
Indicates pipeline stability. Low success rate means flaky tests or unstable code.
Average time from commit to failure detection

Time from commit to production deployment

Bugs found in production vs. testing
Shows testing effectiveness. High escape rate indicates test coverage gaps.

Percentage of builds using cached dependencies
High cache hits speed up builds and reduce resource costs.
Number of commits per day per developer
Measures CI adoption. Low frequency suggests developers aren't integrating regularly.
When in pipeline failures typically occur
Fast-failing pipelines save resources. Fail early, fail fast.
Time to run full test suite
Slow tests are often skipped. Invest in test optimization.

content.caption: CI Metrics Collection and Dashboard Generation
content.code:
# ci_metrics_collector.py import requests import json import time from datetime import datetime, timedelta from collections import defaultdict import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np # Use a valid matplotlib style plt.style.use('ggplot') class CIMetricsCollector: def __init__(self, github_token, repo_owner, repo_name): self.github_token = github_token self.repo_owner = repo_owner self.repo_name = repo_name self.headers = { 'Authorization': f'token {github_token}', 'Accept': 'application/vnd.github.v3+json' } self.base_url = f'https://api.github.com/repos/{repo_owner}/{repo_name}' def collect_workflow_runs(self, days=30): """Collect workflow run data from GitHub Actions""" since = (datetime.now() - timedelta(days=days)).isoformat() url = f"{self.base_url}/actions/runs" params = { 'created': f'>{since}', 'per_page': 100 } all_runs = [] page = 1 while True: params['page'] = page try: response = requests.get(url, headers=self.headers, params=params) response.raise_for_status() data = response.json() if not data.get('workflow_runs'): break all_runs.extend(data['workflow_runs']) # Check if there are more pages if 'next' not in response.links: break page += 1 except requests.exceptions.RequestException as e: print(f"Error collecting workflow runs: {e}") break return all_runs def calculate_metrics(self, runs): """Calculate CI metrics from workflow runs""" metrics = {} if not runs: return { 'build_success_rate': 0, 'avg_build_duration': 0, 'p95_build_duration': 0, 'failure_by_workflow': {}, 'daily_trends': {}, 'mttr': 0 } # Build success rate total_runs = len(runs) successful_runs = sum(1 for r in runs if r.get('conclusion') == 'success') metrics['build_success_rate'] = (successful_runs / total_runs * 100) if total_runs > 0 else 0 # Build duration durations = [] for run in runs: if run.get('run_started_at') and run.get('updated_at'): try: start = datetime.fromisoformat(run['run_started_at'].replace('Z', '+00:00')) end = datetime.fromisoformat(run['updated_at'].replace('Z', '+00:00')) duration = (end - start).total_seconds() / 60 # minutes durations.append(duration) except (ValueError, TypeError): continue metrics['avg_build_duration'] = sum(durations) / len(durations) if durations else 0 metrics['p95_build_duration'] = sorted(durations)[int(len(durations) * 0.95)] if len(durations) > 0 else 0 # Failure patterns failures = [r for r in runs if r.get('conclusion') in ['failure', 'cancelled', 'timed_out']] failure_by_workflow = defaultdict(int) for f in failures: workflow_name = f.get('name', 'unknown') failure_by_workflow[workflow_name] += 1 metrics['failure_by_workflow'] = dict(failure_by_workflow) # Daily trends runs_by_day = defaultdict(lambda: {'total': 0, 'success': 0, 'failure': 0, 'pending': 0}) for run in runs: if run.get('run_started_at'): day = run['run_started_at'][:10] runs_by_day[day]['total'] += 1 conclusion = run.get('conclusion') if conclusion == 'success': runs_by_day[day]['success'] += 1 elif conclusion in ['failure', 'cancelled', 'timed_out']: runs_by_day[day]['failure'] += 1 else: runs_by_day[day]['pending'] += 1 metrics['daily_trends'] = dict(runs_by_day) # MTTR (Mean Time to Repair) # Find consecutive failures followed by success mttr_values = [] current_failure_start = None sorted_runs = sorted(runs, key=lambda r: r.get('run_started_at', '')) for run in sorted_runs: conclusion = run.get('conclusion') run_start = run.get('run_started_at') if not run_start: continue if conclusion in ['failure', 'cancelled', 'timed_out']: if not current_failure_start: try: current_failure_start = datetime.fromisoformat(run_start.replace('Z', '+00:00')) except (ValueError, TypeError): continue else: if current_failure_start: try: success_time = datetime.fromisoformat(run_start.replace('Z', '+00:00')) repair_time = (success_time - current_failure_start).total_seconds() / 3600 # hours if repair_time > 0: # Only add positive repair times mttr_values.append(repair_time) except (ValueError, TypeError): pass finally: current_failure_start = None metrics['mttr'] = sum(mttr_values) / len(mttr_values) if mttr_values else 0 return metrics def generate_dashboard(self, metrics): """Generate HTML dashboard with visualizations""" # Create DataFrame for trends if metrics['daily_trends']: trends_df = pd.DataFrame([ {'date': day, **stats} for day, stats in metrics['daily_trends'].items() ]) trends_df['date'] = pd.to_datetime(trends_df['date']) trends_df['success_rate'] = (trends_df['success'] / trends_df['total'] * 100).fillna(0) trends_df = trends_df.sort_values('date') # content.title: The Complete CI Best Practices Guide
items: ✅ **Commit Early, Commit Often** – Small, frequent changes are easier to integrate and debug. Aim for multiple commits per day. Each commit should be a logical, self-contained change.
✅ **Keep Builds Fast** – Aim for <10 minutes for the complete pipeline. Slow builds discourage frequent commits. Invest in parallelization, caching, and faster hardware.
✅ **Automate Everything** – From builds to tests to deployment validations. No manual steps in the pipeline. If it can be automated, automate it.
✅ **Fail Fast, Fix Fast** – Stop the line when the build breaks. Make fixing the build the highest priority task. No new work until the build is green.
✅ **Test in Production-like Environments** – Avoid 'works on my machine' issues. Use staging environments that mirror production. Containerization helps here.
✅ **Use Feature Flags** – Deploy code safely without exposing it to all users. This enables trunk-based development and continuous deployment.
✅ **Monitor Pipeline Health** – Metrics should be visible on dashboards. Track success rates, durations, and failure patterns. Act on negative trends.
✅ **Treat Pipeline as Code** – Store pipeline definitions in version control. Review pipeline changes like code changes. This enables traceability and disaster recovery.
✅ **Parallelize Tests** – Use containers/nodes to run tests concurrently. Split tests by category, runtime, or module. Matrix builds are your friend.
✅ **Secure the Pipeline** – Scan dependencies, secrets, and containers continuously. Use SAST, DAST, and dependency scanning tools. Never store secrets in code.
✅ **Cache Dependencies Wisely** – Cache npm, Maven, pip packages to speed up builds. Use checksum-based cache keys. Monitor cache hit rates.
✅ **Isolate Build Environments** – Use containers or VMs to ensure consistent environments. Avoid shared state between builds. Clean up after each run.
✅ **Maintain a Staging Environment** – Deploy to staging after successful CI. Run integration and acceptance tests there. Catch environment-specific issues.
✅ **Practice Blameless Post-Mortems** – When builds fail, focus on process, not people. Use retrospectives to improve the pipeline. Share learnings across teams.
✅ **Keep Dependencies Fresh** – Regularly update dependencies to avoid security vulnerabilities. Automate dependency updates with Dependabot or Renovate.
✅ **Monitor Test Flakiness** – Track flaky tests separately. Quarantine or fix them immediately. Flaky tests destroy trust in the pipeline.
✅ **Use Semantic Versioning** – Version artifacts meaningfully. This enables traceability and rollback. Automate versioning in the pipeline.
✅ **Document the Pipeline** – Keep documentation up to date. New team members should understand how the pipeline works. Pipeline as code helps, but comments matter.
✅ **Review Pipeline Performance** – Regularly audit build times and resource usage. Optimize slow stages. Remove unused steps. The pipeline is a product—maintain it.
✅ **Celebrate Green Builds** – Positive reinforcement matters. Acknowledge when the team keeps the build green. Make pipeline health a team achievement.

content.title: Common CI Anti-Patterns
items: ❌ **The 'Works on My Machine' Syndrome** – Developers don't run tests locally, rely on CI to catch failures. CI becomes a debugging tool, not a validation tool.
❌ **Long-Lived Feature Branches** – Branches lasting weeks or months. Integration becomes painful, and CI provides little value. Practice trunk-based development.
❌ **Ignoring Broken Builds** – Allowing builds to stay red for hours or days. This normalizes failure and erodes discipline. Fix builds immediately.
❌ **The 'Testing Phase' at the End** – Treating testing as a separate phase after development. CI should test continuously, not just at the end.
❌ **Flaky Tests Without Action** – Ignoring intermittent failures. Teams learn to distrust the pipeline. Fix or quarantine flaky tests immediately.
❌ **Overly Long Builds** – Pipelines taking hours to complete. Developers stop waiting for feedback. Invest in optimization aggressively.
❌ **Insufficient Test Coverage** – Low coverage gives false confidence. Tests that don't test anything are worse than no tests. Measure coverage meaningfully.
❌ **Hardcoded Secrets in Pipeline** – Storing credentials in pipeline configuration. This is a major security risk. Use secret management tools.
❌ **No Local Testing** – Developers rely entirely on CI to catch errors. This creates long feedback loops. Encourage local testing with pre-commit hooks.
❌ **Pipeline Sprawl** – Too many similar pipelines that are hard to maintain. Use templates, shared libraries, and reusable actions. Consolidate where possible.
❌ **Ignoring Infrastructure** – Treating CI infrastructure as an afterthought. Slow runners, full disks, network issues plague the team. Invest in robust infrastructure.
❌ **No Visibility** – Pipeline status hidden from the team. Dashboards not maintained. Make pipeline health visible to everyone, all the time.

content.title: Netflix's CI Journey
content.scenario: Netflix's CI/CD platform handles thousands of daily deployments across 1,000+ microservices. Their Spinnaker-based platform integrates with Jenkins and GitHub Actions.
content.details:
**The Challenge:**
- 1,000+ microservices with independent release cycles
- Thousands of engineers committing daily
- Need for zero-downtime deployments
- Global infrastructure across multiple regions

**The Solution:**
1. **Spinnaker as CD Platform** – Netflix built Spinnaker (now open-source) to handle multi-cloud deployments
2. **Jenkins for CI** – Each service has its own Jenkins pipeline
3. **Automated Canary Analysis** – Machine learning detects performance regressions
4. **Chaos Engineering** – Automated chaos testing (Chaos Monkey) validates resilience

**Key Practices:**
- **Trunk-Based Development** – All developers commit to main, use feature flags
- **Automated Testing Pyramid** – Extensive unit tests, integration tests, and canary analysis
- **Immutable Infrastructure** – Every deployment creates new instances, no in-place updates
- **Real-Time Monitoring** – Metrics from every deployment feed back into CI decisions

**Results:**
- 4,000+ deployments per day
- 99.99% availability despite constant change
- Rollbacks in under 5 minutes when issues detected
- 80% reduction in deployment-related incidents

content.title: Google's Blaze/Bazel System
content.scenario: Google's monorepo contains billions of lines of code with thousands of daily commits. Their CI system must scale massively while maintaining fast feedback.
content.details:
**The Challenge:**
- Single repository with all of Google's code
- 25,000+ engineers committing daily
- 50,000+ commits per day
- Build and test across multiple languages and platforms

**The Solution:**
1. **Bazel Build System** – Google built Blaze (open-sourced as Bazel) for hermetic, reproducible builds
2. **Distributed Build Execution** – Builds distributed across thousands of machines
3. **Test Impact Analysis** – Only tests affected by changes are run
4. **Remote Caching** – Build artifacts cached globally

**Key Technologies:**
- **Bazel** – Build and test with precise dependency analysis
- **RBE (Remote Build Execution)** – Distributed build farm
- **Test Scheduler** – Prioritizes and parallelizes test execution
- **Code Search & Cross-Reference** – Enables understanding across codebase

**Results:**
- 99% of builds complete in under 5 minutes
- Trillions of test cases executed daily
- 80% reduction in build time through caching
- Developers get feedback within minutes for most changes

content.title: Etsy's Deploy Culture
content.scenario: Etsy is known for rapid deployments (50+ per day). Their CI pipeline emphasizes fast rollback mechanisms and feature flagging to reduce risk.
content.details:
**The Culture:**
- 'Deploy whenever you want' philosophy
- Engineers own their code from commit to production
- Blameless post-mortems for incidents
- Metrics-driven decision making

**Key Practices:**
1. **Feature Flags** – New features hidden behind flags, enabled gradually
2. **Automated Testing** – Comprehensive test suite runs on every commit
3. **Deployinator** – Custom deployment tool with one-click rollback
4. **ChatOps** – Deployments triggered and monitored via chat
5. **Dark Launches** – Run new code in production without exposing to users

**Pipeline Design:**
- Commit triggers Jenkins build
- Unit tests run (2-3 minutes)
- Integration tests in staging (5 minutes)
- Canary deployment to 1% of servers
- Monitor metrics for 5 minutes
- Gradual rollout to remaining servers

**Results:**
- 50+ deployments per day
- Mean time to recovery under 10 minutes
- 90% of commits reach production within 24 hours
- Developer satisfaction consistently high

content.title: HIPAA-Compliant CI Pipeline
content.scenario: A healthcare SaaS company needed to maintain HIPAA compliance while accelerating development. They integrated TestRail with Jenkins, ensuring every regulatory compliance test runs before releases.
content.details:
**The Challenge:**
- HIPAA compliance requirements
- Sensitive patient data
- Audit trails for all changes
- 50+ regulated controls to verify

**The Solution:**
1. **TestRail Integration** – Manual test cases tracked in TestRail, triggered by Jenkins
2. **Automated Compliance Checks** – Scripts verify PHI handling, encryption, access controls
3. **Audit Logging** – Every CI action logged for compliance reviews
4. **Approval Gates** – Manual approvals required for production deployments

**Pipeline Stages:**
```
Commit → Build → Unit Tests → Integration Tests → 
Compliance Scan → Security Scan → Manual Approval → 
Staging Deploy → UAT Tests → Production Deploy
```

**Results:**
- 40% reduction in defect escape rate
- Compliance audit time reduced from 2 weeks to 2 days
- 100% traceability from commit to production
- Passed HIPAA audit with zero findings

content.title: Global Bank's DevSecOps Transformation
content.scenario: A global bank used CI pipelines with SonarQube, Checkmarx, and Zephyr for compliance. Build duration reduced from 4 hours to 30 minutes with containerized pipelines.
content.details:
**The Challenge:**
- Strict regulatory requirements (PCI-DSS, SOX)
- 200+ microservices with frequent updates
- Need for fast feedback while maintaining security
- Legacy build infrastructure (4+ hour builds)

**The Solution:**
1. **Containerized Builds** – Migrated from physical agents to Kubernetes
2. **Parallel Security Scanning** – SAST, DAST, and dependency scans run in parallel
3. **Test Impact Analysis** – Only run tests affected by changes
4. **Quality Gates** – Automatic failure if coverage drops or vulnerabilities found

**Security Integration:**
- **SAST** – Checkmarx scans for code vulnerabilities
- **DAST** – OWASP ZAP scans running applications
- **SCA** – Black Duck for dependency scanning
- **Secret Scanning** – TruffleHog detects secrets in code
- **Container Scanning** – Twistlock scans Docker images

**Results:**
- Build duration reduced from 4 hours to 30 minutes
- 95% of security issues caught before staging
- Zero critical security incidents in 2 years
- Developer productivity increased by 300%

content.title: Taming Flaky Tests
content.explanation:
Flaky tests are the #1 enemy of reliable CI pipelines. They undermine trust, waste time, and hide real failures. A comprehensive strategy is needed to manage them.

**What Makes Tests Flaky?**
- **Timing Issues** – Race conditions, async operations
- **Order Dependencies** – Tests that assume a specific order
- **External Dependencies** – Network calls, APIs, databases
- **Resource Leaks** – Memory, file handles, connections
- **Random Data** – Non-deterministic test data
- **Environment Differences** – Different OS, locale, timezone
- **Concurrency Issues** – Parallel test interference

**Flaky Test Management Strategy:**

1. **Detection**
   - Track test results over time
   - Flag tests that pass and fail on same code
   - Use tools like Test Analytics, Flaky Test Detector

2. **Quarantine**
   - Move flaky tests to separate suite
   - Don't block CI on quarantined tests
   - Track flakiness metrics

3. **Analysis**
   - Investigate root causes
   - Review test implementation
   - Look for timing, order, or data issues

4. **Fix or Delete**
   - Fix the test or the code
   - If can't fix, delete the test
   - Document decisions

5. **Prevention**
   - Code review guidelines for tests
   - Training on test design
   - Tools to prevent common flaky patterns

content.title: The Next Generation of CI
items: 🤖 **AI-Powered CI** – Machine learning models predict flaky tests, auto-optimize build parallelization, suggest fixes for failing builds, and prioritize test execution based on risk analysis.
📦 **GitOps Integration** – CI pipelines triggering GitOps-style deployments where infrastructure state is managed through Git. CI validates changes, GitOps applies them.
🔒 **Shift-Left Security (DevSecOps)** – Security integrated throughout the pipeline. SAST, DAST, SCA, and container scanning run automatically. Security gates at every stage.
⚡ **Serverless CI/CD** – Event-driven, scalable pipelines with zero infrastructure management. Pay only for what you use. Auto-scaling to handle peak loads.
🌍 **Edge CI/CD** – Deploying builds/tests closer to where users are. Testing at edge locations for latency-sensitive applications. CDN-based testing.
☁️ **Hybrid and Multi-Cloud CI** – Pipelines designed to span across cloud providers and on-premises infrastructure. Vendor-agnostic pipelines.
🎯 **Test Impact Analysis Everywhere** – AI-powered analysis of code changes to determine exactly which tests need to run. Eliminates unnecessary test execution.
🔄 **Self-Healing Pipelines** – Pipelines that automatically detect and recover from failures. Auto-retry flaky tests, provision new agents when nodes fail.
📊 **Unified Observability** – Metrics, logs, and traces from CI pipelines integrated with application monitoring. End-to-end visibility from commit to production.
🔧 **Pipeline as Product** – Treating CI pipelines as products with dedicated teams, roadmaps, and user feedback. Internal developer platforms for CI/CD.
🎨 **Low-Code/No-Code CI** – Visual pipeline builders for non-experts. Templates and wizards for common scenarios. Democratizing CI/CD.
🔐 **Supply Chain Security** – SBOM generation, dependency verification, signed commits, and attestations integrated into CI. Protecting software supply chains.
📈 **Predictive Analytics** – Predicting build failures before they happen. Identifying risky commits. Suggesting preventive actions.
🔄 **Continuous Feedback** – Pipelines that provide richer feedback: code suggestions, performance insights, security recommendations, all in the developer's workflow.
🌐 **Universal CI** – Single pipeline that works across any language, any platform, any cloud. No more re-inventing pipelines per project.

tutorials.title: 🚀 Continuous Delivery (CD)
tutorials.description: Master Continuous Delivery (CD) to ensure every code change is production-ready. Learn how to automate deployment pipelines, implement deployment strategies, and build a culture of reliable, frequent releases that deliver value to users faster and safer.

content.title: Defining Continuous Delivery
content.explanation:
Continuous Delivery (CD) is a software development practice where every code change is built, tested, and prepared for release to production. It extends Continuous Integration by ensuring that the software is always in a deployable state, enabling teams to release at any time with minimal manual effort.

At its core, CD is about **making deployments boring**. In traditional software delivery, deployments were rare, high-risk events that required extensive planning, late nights, and heroics. CD flips this model by making deployments frequent, automated, and routine—so routine that they become unremarkable.

**The CD Mindset:**
- Deployments should be low-risk and reversible
- Quality is built in, not tacked on at the end
- Feedback loops should be short and actionable
- Everyone shares responsibility for deliverability

**Key Distinctions:**
- **Continuous Delivery** – Code is always deployable, but may require manual approval for production
- **Continuous Deployment** – Every change that passes tests is automatically deployed to production

content.text: Continuous Delivery is the ability to get changes of all types—including new features, configuration changes, bug fixes and experiments—into production, or into the hands of users, safely and quickly in a sustainable way.

items.definition: Every commit results in a potentially shippable product. Teams should be able to deploy to production with a single click at any moment.
All steps from commit to deployment are automated—build, test, deploy, verify, and rollback if necessary.
Development, staging, and production environments are as similar as possible to prevent environment-specific issues.
Deployments follow the same process every time, eliminating manual steps that introduce variability and errors.
Metrics, logs, and monitoring provide immediate insight into the health of deployments and applications.
Security checks are automated throughout the pipeline, not performed as a final gate.

content.value:
**When to use each approach:**

- **CI only**: Teams just starting with automation, small projects, or when regulatory requirements don't permit frequent releases
- **Continuous Delivery**: Most teams—balances automation with control, allows business to decide release timing
- **Continuous Deployment**: SaaS companies, teams with high test coverage and confidence, when rapid iteration is critical

content.title: Why Organizations Invest in CD
items: **📈 Faster Time to Market** – Features reach users in days instead of months, enabling rapid response to market changes and competitive pressure.
**💰 Reduced Cost of Release** – Automated pipelines eliminate manual effort, reducing the cost of each release by 50-80%.
**🎯 Lower Risk** – Small, frequent changes are easier to validate and roll back. Failed deployments affect fewer users and are fixed faster.
**📊 Better Quality** – Automated testing catches defects early. Continuous feedback from users improves product-market fit.
**😊 Happier Teams** – No more late-night deployment marathons. Developers focus on features, not firefighting. Teams gain confidence and morale.
**🔒 Improved Security** – Security checks automated throughout the pipeline. Faster patching of vulnerabilities.
**📋 Regulatory Compliance** – Automated audit trails show exactly what changed, who approved it, and when it deployed.
**🚀 Innovation Velocity** – Experiment freely with feature flags and A/B testing. Learn from real user behavior and iterate quickly.

content.value:
The concept of Continuous Delivery emerged from the Agile and Lean software development movements of the early 2000s. Key influences include:

**Extreme Programming (XP)** – Practices like continuous integration and small releases laid the groundwork.

**Lean Manufacturing** – Principles from Toyota's production system (just-in-time, stopping the line, continuous improvement) inspired software delivery thinking.

**The Agile Manifesto** (2001) – Values like 'working software over comprehensive documentation' and 'responding to change over following a plan' emphasized frequent delivery.

The DevOps movement of the late 2000s was crucial to CD's development. By breaking down silos between development and operations, DevOps enabled the automation and collaboration needed for continuous delivery.

**Key milestones:**
- **2006** – The term 'DevOps' is coined by Patrick Debois and Andrew Clay Shafer
- **2009** – First DevOpsDays conference in Ghent
- **2010** – 'Continuous Delivery' book published by Jez Humble and Dave Farley, codifying principles and practices

content.title: Understanding Pipeline Stages
content.explanation:
A CD pipeline is an automated sequence of stages that code passes through on its journey from commit to production. Each stage increases confidence that the software is safe to release. The pipeline acts as a factory assembly line for software, with quality checks at every step.

**Key characteristics of effective pipelines:**
- **Fast** – Feedback within minutes, not hours
- **Reliable** – Results are consistent and trustworthy
- **Repeatable** – Same commit produces same result every time
- **Visible** – Everyone can see status and logs
- **Safe** – Automatic rollback on failure
- **Auditable** – Complete trail of what, when, and who

- Resource usage monitoring
- Often runs less frequently (e.g., nightly)

Final checkpoint before production:
- Manual approval for regulated industries
- Business stakeholder sign-off
- Compliance checks
- Can be skipped for fully automated deployments

Safe deployment to production:
- Use deployment strategy (blue-green, canary, rolling)
- Automate the entire process
- Monitor for errors
- Have automatic rollback triggers

Confirm the deployment succeeded:
- Smoke tests against production
- Health check monitoring
- Error rate tracking
- Performance comparison
- User feedback collection

content.title: Zero-Downtime with Blue-Green
content.explanation:
Blue-Green deployment maintains two identical production environments: Blue (current) and Green (new). At any time, only one environment serves live traffic. When deploying a new version, you deploy to the inactive environment, test it, then switch traffic.

**How it works:**
1. Blue environment serves production traffic
2. Deploy new version to Green environment
3. Run tests against Green to verify
4. Switch router/load balancer from Blue to Green
5. If issues arise, switch back to Blue immediately

**Advantages:**
- Instant switch with zero downtime
- Immediate rollback (just flip the switch back)
- Can run smoke tests before switching
- Both environments identical

**Challenges:**
- Requires double the infrastructure cost
- Database schema changes need careful handling
- State must be shared or migrated carefully
- Session data needs to be considered

content.title: Blue-Green Deployment Flow
content.caption: Traffic switches instantly from Blue to Green environment

layers.activity: Users → Load Balancer → Blue (v1) → Database
Deploy v2 to Green, run tests, database migrations
Users → Load Balancer → Green (v2) → Database
Switch back to Blue, Blue still has v1 running

content.caption: Blue-Green Deployment Script
content.code:
#!/bin/bash
# blue-green-deploy.sh

set -e

# Configuration
APP_NAME="myapp"
BLUE_ENV="blue"
GREEN_ENV="green"
ACTIVE_ENV_FILE="/etc/nginx/active-env.txt"
NGINX_CONFIG="/etc/nginx/sites-enabled/myapp.conf"

# Function to get current active environment
get_active_env() {
    if [ -f "$ACTIVE_ENV_FILE" ]; then
        cat "$ACTIVE_ENV_FILE"
    else
        echo "blue"
    fi
}

# Function to switch traffic to specified environment
switch_traffic() {
    local target_env=$1
    echo "Switching traffic to $target_env environment..."
    
    # Update Nginx config to point to target environment
    sed -i "s/server blue.*;/server $target_env:8080;/g" $NGINX_CONFIG
    
    # Reload Nginx to apply changes
    nginx -s reload
    
    # Save active environment
    echo "$target_env" > $ACTIVE_ENV_FILE
    
    echo "Traffic switched to $target_env"
}

# Main deployment script
deploy() {
    local version=$1
    local target_env=$2
    
    echo "Deploying version $version to $target_env..."
    
    # Pull new image
    docker pull myapp:$version
    
    # Stop and remove old container if exists
    docker stop $APP_NAME-$target_env || true
    docker rm $APP_NAME-$target_env || true
    
    # Start new container
    docker run -d \
        --name $APP_NAME-$target_env \
        --network myapp-network \
        -e NODE_ENV=production \
        -e DATABASE_URL=$DATABASE_URL \
        myapp:$version
    
    # Wait for container to be healthy
    echo "Waiting for container to be healthy..."
    for i in {1..30}; do
        if docker exec $APP_NAME-$target_env curl -f http://localhost:8080/health; then
            echo "Container is healthy!"
            break
        fi
        sleep 2
    done
    
    echo "Deployment to $target_env complete"
}

# Rollback function
rollback() {
    local current_env=$(get_active_env)
    local previous_env=$([ "$current_env" == "blue" ] && echo "green" || echo "blue")
    
    echo "Rolling back from $current_env to $previous_env..."
    switch_traffic $previous_env
    echo "Rollback complete"
}

# Main execution
main() {
    local VERSION=$1
    local ACTION=${2:-"deploy"}
    
    if [ "$ACTION" == "deploy" ]; then
        # Determine inactive environment
        local ACTIVE_ENV=$(get_active_env)
        local TARGET_ENV=$([ "$ACTIVE_ENV" == "blue" ] && echo "green" || echo "blue")
        
        echo "Active environment: $ACTIVE_ENV"
        echo "Target environment: $TARGET_ENV"
        
        # Deploy to inactive environment
        deploy $VERSION $TARGET_ENV
        
        # Run smoke tests
        echo "Running smoke tests on $TARGET_ENV..."
        npm run test:smoke -- --url=http://$TARGET_ENV:8080
        
        # Switch traffic
        switch_traffic $TARGET_ENV
        
        echo "Deployment successful!"
        
    elif [ "$ACTION" == "rollback" ]; then
        rollback
    fi
}

# Run main function with arguments
main "$@"

content.title: Gradual Rollout with Canaries
content.explanation:
Canary deployment gradually rolls out a new version to a small subset of users before full deployment. Named after 'canary in a coal mine,' this strategy detects issues early with minimal impact.

**How it works:**
1. Deploy new version alongside old version
2. Route small percentage of traffic (e.g., 5%) to canary
3. Monitor metrics (errors, latency, business metrics)
4. If canary performs well, gradually increase traffic
5. If issues detected, stop canary and roll back

**Traffic Progression:**
- Phase 1: 5% canary, 95% stable
- Phase 2: 20% canary, 80% stable
- Phase 3: 50% canary, 50% stable
- Phase 4: 100% new version

**Advantages:**
- Minimal risk – issues affect only small user subset
- Real user monitoring with actual traffic
- Canary analysis can be automated
- Gradual rollout allows early detection

**Challenges:**
- Requires sophisticated traffic routing
- Metrics must be statistically significant
- Session consistency may be needed
- Complex to implement manually

content.caption: Canary Deployment in Kubernetes with Istio
content.code:
# canary-kubernetes.yaml
---
# Stable deployment (v1)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: myapp-v1
  labels:
    app: myapp
    version: v1
spec:
  replicas: 9
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: myapp
      version: v1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: myapp
        version: v1
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: myapp
        image: myapp:1.0.0
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
---
# Canary deployment (v2)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: myapp-v2
  labels:
    app: myapp
    version: v2
spec:
  replicas: 1  # 10% canary (1 of 10 total)
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: myapp
      version: v2
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: myapp
        version: v2
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: myapp
        image: myapp:2.0.0
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
---
# Service for both versions
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: myapp-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: myapp
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 8080
---
# Istio VirtualService for traffic splitting
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: myapp
spec:
  hosts:
  - myapp-service
  http:
  - match:
    - headers:
        x-canary:
          exact: "true"
    route:
    - destination:
        host: myapp-service
        subset: v2
      weight: 100
  - route:
    - destination:
        host: myapp-service
        subset: v1
      weight: 90
    - destination:
        host: myapp-service
        subset: v2
      weight: 10
---
# DestinationRule for subsets
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: myapp
spec:
  host: myapp-service
  subsets:
  - name: v1
    labels:
      version: v1
  - name: v2
    labels:
      version: v2
---
# Canary analysis job
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: canary-analysis
spec:
  schedule: "*/5 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          containers:
          - name: analyzer
            image: prom/prometheus:v2.45.0
            command:
            - /bin/sh
            - -c
            - |
              # Query error rates for both versions
              V1_ERRORS=$(curl -s 'http://prometheus:9090/api/v1/query?query=sum(rate(http_requests_total{version="v1",status=~"5.."}[5m]))' | jq '.data.result[0].value[1]')
              V2_ERRORS=$(curl -s 'http://prometheus:9090/api/v1/query?query=sum(rate(http_requests_total{version="v2",status=~"5.."}[5m]))' | jq '.data.result[0].value[1]')
              
              # Compare error rates
              if (( $(echo "$V2_ERRORS > $V1_ERRORS * 2" | bc -l) )); then
                echo "Canary error rate too high! Rolling back..."
                # Trigger rollback (e.g., via Argo Rollouts)
                kubectl argo rollouts abort myapp
              else
                echo "Canary healthy. Consider increasing traffic."
                # Gradually increase canary weight
                CURRENT_WEIGHT=$(kubectl get virtualservice myapp -o json | jq '.spec.http[1].route[1].weight')
                NEW_WEIGHT=$((CURRENT_WEIGHT + 10))
                if [ $NEW_WEIGHT -le 100 ]; then
                  kubectl patch virtualservice myapp --type='json' \
                    -p='[{"op": "replace", "path": "/spec/http/1/route/1/weight", "value": '$NEW_WEIGHT'}]'
                fi
              fi
          restartPolicy: OnFailure

content.title: Gradual Instance Replacement
content.explanation:
Rolling updates gradually replace instances of the old version with the new version, one by one. This is the default strategy in many orchestrators like Kubernetes.

**How it works:**
1. Start with all instances running version v1
2. Bring down one v1 instance
3. Bring up one v2 instance
4. Wait for it to become healthy
5. Repeat until all instances are v2

**Configuration options:**
- **maxSurge** – How many extra instances can be created (e.g., 25%)
- **maxUnavailable** – How many instances can be down during update (e.g., 25%)
- **minReadySeconds** – Wait time before considering instance healthy

**Advantages:**
- No downtime if configured correctly
- No additional infrastructure cost
- Works with any infrastructure
- Simple to understand and implement

**Challenges:**
- Slower than blue-green (takes time to roll through)
- During update, both versions run simultaneously
- May need to handle version compatibility
- Rollback also takes time

content.caption: Rolling Update in Kubernetes
content.code:
# rolling-update.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: myapp
spec:
  replicas: 10
  # Rolling update strategy configuration
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 2        # Can create 2 extra pods during update
      maxUnavailable: 1  # Can have 1 pod unavailable during update
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: myapp
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: myapp
        version: v2
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: myapp
        image: myapp:2.0.0
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 5
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "256Mi"
            cpu: "250m"
          limits:
            memory: "512Mi"
            cpu: "500m"
---
# Command to trigger rolling update
# kubectl set image deployment/myapp myapp=myapp:2.0.0
#
# Monitor rollout status
# kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp
#
# Pause rollout if issues detected
# kubectl rollout pause deployment/myapp
#
# Resume rollout
# kubectl rollout resume deployment/myapp
#
# Rollback if needed
# kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp

content.title: Release Without Deployment
content.explanation:
Feature flags (or feature toggles) allow you to turn features on or off without deploying new code. This decouples deployment from release—you can deploy code with features hidden behind flags and enable them later.

**How it works:**
1. Wrap new features in conditional checks
2. Store flag configurations in a central system
3. Deploy code with flags OFF
4. Enable flags gradually for users
5. Monitor and adjust in real-time

**Flag Types:**
- **Release Toggles** – Control feature visibility
- **Experiment Toggles** – A/B testing variants
- **Ops Toggles** – Circuit breakers, kill switches
- **Permission Toggles** – Premium features per user

**Advantages:**
- Separate deployment from release
- Instant on/off without redeploy
- Canary releases per user segment
- Trunk-based development enabled
- Easy A/B testing

**Challenges:**
- Flag management complexity
- Need to clean up old flags
- Potential technical debt
- Testing matrix grows

content.title: GitOps: The Git-as-Truth Approach
content.explanation:
GitOps is a modern approach to Continuous Delivery where Git serves as the single source of truth for declarative infrastructure and applications. With GitOps, the desired state of the system is stored in Git, and automated operators synchronize the live environment to match that state.

**How GitOps Works:**
1. All configuration (Kubernetes YAML, Helm charts, Kustomize) stored in Git
2. CI pipeline builds and tests application
3. CI pipeline updates configuration in Git repository (e.g., changes image tag)
4. GitOps operator (Argo CD, Flux) detects change
5. Operator synchronizes live environment with Git state

**Benefits of GitOps:**
- **Single source of truth** – Git contains everything
- **Audit trail** – Every change is tracked
- **Easy rollback** – Revert Git commit
- **Disaster recovery** – Recreate cluster from Git
- **Pull-based deployments** – More secure
- **Self-healing** – Corrects drift automatically

**Argo CD Features:**
- Automated sync to desired state
- Sync strategies (auto, manual, scheduled)
- Health assessment of resources
- Rollback capabilities
- SSO integration
- Web UI and CLI
- Multi-cluster management

content.caption: Argo CD Application Definition
content.code:
# argocd-application.yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: myapp-production
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  # Source repository
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/myorg/myapp-config.git
    targetRevision: HEAD
    path: k8s/overlays/production
    # Use Helm if needed
    helm:
      valueFiles:
        - values-production.yaml
      parameters:
        - name: image.tag
          value: v1.2.3
  
  # Destination cluster
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: production
  
  # Sync policy
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true  # Remove resources not in Git
      selfHeal: true  # Correct drift
      allowEmpty: false
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true
      - ApplyOutOfSyncOnly=true
    retry:
      limit: 5
      backoff:
        duration: 5s
        factor: 2
        maxDuration: 3m
  
  # Sync waves and hooks
  sync:
    hooks:
      - name: pre-sync-db-migration
        manifest: |
          apiVersion: batch/v1
          kind: Job
          metadata:
            name: db-migration
            namespace: production
            annotations:
              argocd.argoproj.io/hook: PreSync
          spec:
            template:
              spec:
                restartPolicy: Never
                containers:
                - name: migrate
                  image: myapp:migration-tool
                  envFrom:
                  - secretRef:
                      name: db-secret
  
  # Health checks
  ignoreDifferences:
    - group: apps
      kind: Deployment
      jsonPointers:
        - /spec/replicas  # Ignore replica count differences
  
  # Notifications
  notifications:
    - trigger: on-sync-succeeded
      destinations:
        - slack: #deployments
      message: "{{.app.metadata.name}} synced successfully"

---
# Argo CD Project (for multi-team setup)
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AppProject
metadata:
  name: production-apps
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  # Source repositories allowed
  sourceRepos:
    - 'https://github.com/myorg/*'
  
  # Destination clusters and namespaces
  destinations:
    - namespace: production
      server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    - namespace: staging
      server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
  
  # Allowed resources
  clusterResourceWhitelist:
    - group: ''
      kind: Namespace
  
  # RBAC
  roles:
    - name: developer
      description: Developer access
      policies:
        - p, proj:production-apps:developer, applications, get, production-apps/*, allow
        - p, proj:production-apps:developer, applications, sync, production-apps/*, allow
      groups:
        - myorg-developers
    
    - name: release-manager
      description: Release manager access
      policies:
        - p, proj:production-apps:release-manager, applications, *, production-apps/*, allow
      groups:
        - myorg-release-managers

content.caption: Argo Rollouts with Canary Analysis
content.code:
# argo-rollout.yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: myapp-rollout
spec:
  replicas: 10
  strategy:
    canary:
      # Canary steps
      steps:
      - setWeight: 10
      - pause: {duration: 5m}
      - setWeight: 20
      - pause: {duration: 5m}
      - setWeight: 40
      - pause: {duration: 5m}
      - setWeight: 60
      - pause: {duration: 5m}
      - setWeight: 80
      - pause: {duration: 5m}
      - setWeight: 100
      
      # Analysis configuration
      analysis:
        templates:
        - templateName: success-rate
        - templateName: error-rate
        - templateName: latency
        startingStep: 2  # Start analysis after 20% weight
        args:
        - name: service-name
          value: myapp-service
      
      # Traffic routing (with Istio)
      trafficRouting:
        istio:
          virtualService:
            name: myapp-vsvc
            routes:
            - primary
          destinationRule:
            name: myapp-destination
            canarySubsetName: canary
            stableSubsetName: stable
  
  # Pod template
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: myapp
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: myapp
        image: myapp:2.0.0
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080

---
# AnalysisTemplate for success rate
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AnalysisTemplate
metadata:
  name: success-rate
spec:
  args:
  - name: service-name
  metrics:
  - name: success-rate
    interval: 1m
    successCondition: result[0] >= 0.95
    failureCondition: result[0] < 0.90
    provider:
      prometheus:
        address: http://prometheus:9090
        query: |
          sum(rate(
            http_requests_total{
              service="{{args.service-name}}",
              status=~"2.*"
            }[1m]
          )) /
          sum(rate(
            http_requests_total{
              service="{{args.service-name}}"
            }[1m]
          ))

---
# AnalysisTemplate for latency
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AnalysisTemplate
metadata:
  name: latency
spec:
  args:
  - name: service-name
  metrics:
  - name: p95-latency
    interval: 1m
    successCondition: result[0] <= 500
    provider:
      prometheus:
        address: http://prometheus:9090
        query: |
          histogram_quantile(0.95,
            sum(rate(
              http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{
                service="{{args.service-name}}"
              }[1m]
            )) by (le)
          ) * 1000

---
# VirtualService for traffic splitting
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: myapp-vsvc
spec:
  hosts:
  - myapp
  http:
  - name: primary
    route:
    - destination:
        host: myapp
        subset: stable
      weight: 90
    - destination:
        host: myapp
        subset: canary
      weight: 10

---
# DestinationRule
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: myapp-destination
spec:
  host: myapp
  subsets:
  - name: stable
    labels:
      app: myapp
      rollouts-pod-template-hash: stable-hash
  - name: canary
    labels:
      app: myapp
      rollouts-pod-template-hash: canary-hash
  trafficPolicy:
    connectionPool:
      tcp:
        maxConnections: 100

content.title: The CD Manifesto: Principles for Success
items: ✅ **Automate Everything** – Build, test, deploy, rollback, and verify. No manual steps in production path.
✅ **Build Quality In** – Test at every stage. Don't rely on final QA gate.
✅ **Keep Environments Identical** – Use containers, infrastructure as code, and config management.
✅ **Deploy the Same Way Everywhere** – Same scripts, same tools, same process from dev to prod.
✅ **Make Rollbacks Easy** – Every deployment should be reversible in seconds, not hours.
✅ **Use Feature Flags** – Decouple deployment from release. Turn features on/off without code changes.
✅ **Monitor Everything** – Metrics, logs, traces for every deployment. Know immediately if something breaks.
✅ **Start Small, Deploy Often** – Small changes are easier to validate and roll back.
✅ **Practice Blameless Post-Mortems** – When deployments fail, focus on process, not people.
✅ **Treat Pipeline as Code** – Version control, review, and test pipeline changes like application code.
✅ **Secure the Pipeline** – Scan dependencies, secrets, containers. Use least-privilege access.
✅ **Measure and Improve** – Track deployment frequency, lead time, MTTR, change failure rate.
✅ **Use Deployment Strategies** – Choose blue-green, canary, or rolling based on risk tolerance.
✅ **Validate Before Full Rollout** – Smoke tests, canary analysis, automated verification.
✅ **Document the Process** – Keep runbooks updated. New team members should understand the pipeline.
✅ **Celebrate Success** – Acknowledge smooth deployments. Build a culture of confidence.

content.title: CD Anti-Patterns to Avoid
items: ❌ **Big Bang Releases** – Deploying months of changes at once. Invites disaster.
❌ **Environment Drift** – Staging different from production. Leads to 'works in staging' failures.
❌ **Manual Deployment Steps** – Forgotten steps, typos, inconsistencies. Automate everything.
❌ **Skipping Tests** – 'We'll test in production' is not a strategy.
❌ **No Rollback Plan** – Every deployment should have a tested rollback procedure.
❌ **Infrequent Deployments** – If you deploy rarely, each deployment becomes high-risk.
❌ **Long-Lived Branches** – Merge conflicts, integration hell. Practice trunk-based development.
❌ **Ignoring Pipeline Failures** – Red builds become normal. Fix failures immediately.
❌ **Hardcoded Configurations** – Config in code, not in environment variables.
❌ **Deploying During Business Hours** – Users shouldn't see errors. Use zero-downtime strategies.
❌ **No Monitoring** – Deploy and hope for the best. Always monitor after deployment.
❌ **Siloed Teams** – Devs build, Ops deploy. Break down walls with DevOps culture.

content.title: Netflix's CD Journey
content.scenario: Netflix deploys thousands of times per day across 1,000+ microservices with Spinnaker, their open-source CD platform.
content.details:
**The Challenge:**
- 1,000+ microservices with independent release cycles
- Global infrastructure across multiple regions
- Need for zero-downtime deployments
- Handling billions of streaming hours

**The Solution:**
1. **Spinnaker** – Multi-cloud CD platform with blue-green and canary deployments
2. **Automated Canary Analysis** – Kayenta project for ML-based canary analysis
3. **Chaos Engineering** – Chaos Monkey tests resilience by randomly terminating instances
4. **Global Deployments** – Staged rollouts across regions

**Key Practices:**
- **Immutable Infrastructure** – Every deployment creates new instances
- **Automated Rollbacks** – Instant rollback on metrics degradation
- **Red/Black Deployments** – Netflix's term for blue-green
- **Real-Time Monitoring** – Atlas telemetry system

**Results:**
- Thousands of deployments per day
- 99.99% availability
- Deployments in under 15 minutes
- 80% reduction in deployment-related incidents

content.title: Etsy's Deploy Culture
content.scenario: Etsy has been practicing continuous deployment since 2009, deploying 50+ times per day with a strong culture of developer ownership.
content.details:
**The Culture:**
- 'Deploy whenever you want' philosophy
- Engineers own their code from commit to production
- Blameless post-mortems for incidents
- Metrics-driven decision making

**Key Practices:**
1. **Feature Flags** – New features hidden behind flags
2. **Deployinator** – Custom deployment tool with one-click rollback
3. **ChatOps** – Deployments triggered via chat
4. **Dark Launches** – Run new code without exposing to users
5. **Canary Testing** – Deploy to 1% of servers first

**Pipeline Design:**
- Commit triggers Jenkins build
- Unit tests run (2-3 minutes)
- Integration tests in staging (5 minutes)
- Canary deployment to 1% of servers
- Monitor metrics for 5 minutes
- Gradual rollout to remaining servers

**Results:**
- 50+ deployments per day
- Mean time to recovery under 10 minutes
- 90% of commits reach production within 24 hours
- Developer satisfaction consistently high

content.title: Capital One's CD Transformation
content.scenario: Capital One transformed from traditional quarterly releases to continuous delivery while maintaining banking compliance.
content.details:
**The Challenge:**
- Strict regulatory requirements (SOX, PCI-DSS)
- Need for audit trails on all changes
- Legacy monolith applications
- Security concerns with frequent releases

**The Solution:**
1. **Automated Compliance Checks** – Compliance as code in pipelines
2. **Immutable Audit Logs** – Every deployment recorded immutably
3. **Approval Gates** – Automated checks plus manual approval
4. **Container Strategy** – Consistent environments for compliance

**Security Integration:**
- SAST, DAST, and dependency scanning in pipeline
- Secrets management with HashiCorp Vault
- Signed commits and containers
- Automated policy enforcement

**Results:**
- Deployment frequency increased 10x
- Audit time reduced from weeks to hours
- 100% traceability from commit to production
- Passed all regulatory audits
