content.code:
# alerting_rules.yml

groups:
  - name: performance_alerts
    interval: 30s
    rules:
      # High response time alerts
      - alert: HighResponseTimeP95
        expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, service)) > 0.5
        for: 5m
        labels:
          severity: warning
        annotations:
          summary: "{{ $labels.service }} has high p95 response time"
          description: "p95 response time for {{ $labels.service }} is {{ $value }}s (threshold 0.5s)"
      
      - alert: CriticalResponseTimeP99
        expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, service)) > 2
        for: 2m
        labels:
          severity: critical
        annotations:
          summary: "{{ $labels.service }} has critical p99 response time"
          description: "p99 response time for {{ $labels.service }} is {{ $value }}s (threshold 2s)"
      
      # Error rate alerts
      - alert: HighErrorRate
        expr: sum(rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m])) by (service) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m])) by (service) > 0.05
        for: 5m
        labels:
          severity: critical
        annotations:
          summary: "High error rate for {{ $labels.service }}"
          description: "Error rate for {{ $labels.service }} is {{ $value | humanizePercentage }} (threshold 5%)"
      
      # CPU alerts
      - alert: HighCPUUsage
        expr: 100 - (avg by (instance) (rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}[5m])) * 100) > 90
        for: 10m
        labels:
          severity: warning
        annotations:
          summary: "High CPU usage on {{ $labels.instance }}"
          description: "CPU usage is {{ $value }}% (threshold 90%)"
      
      - alert: CriticalCPUUsage
        expr: 100 - (avg by (instance) (rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}[5m])) * 100) > 95
        for: 5m
        labels:
          severity: critical
        annotations:
          summary: "Critical CPU usage on {{ $labels.instance }}"
          description: "CPU usage is {{ $value }}% (threshold 95%)"
      
      # Memory alerts
      - alert: HighMemoryUsage
        expr: (node_memory_MemTotal_bytes - node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes) / node_memory_MemTotal_bytes * 100 > 90
        for: 10m
        labels:
          severity: warning
        annotations:
          summary: "High memory usage on {{ $labels.instance }}"
          description: "Memory usage is {{ $value }}% (threshold 90%)"
      
      - alert: MemoryLeakDetected
        expr: (node_memory_MemTotal_bytes - node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes) / node_memory_MemTotal_bytes * 100 > 80 and predict_linear(node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes[6h], 3600) < 0
        for: 1h
        labels:
          severity: critical
        annotations:
          summary: "Potential memory leak on {{ $labels.instance }}"
          description: "Memory usage trending upward, predicted to exhaust in 1 hour"
      
      # Disk I/O alerts
      - alert: HighDiskIOWait
        expr: rate(node_disk_io_time_seconds_total[5m]) > 0.5
        for: 10m
        labels:
          severity: warning
        annotations:
          summary: "High disk I/O wait on {{ $labels.instance }}"
          description: "Disk I/O wait is {{ $value }}s/s (threshold 0.5s/s)"
      
      - alert: DiskSpaceLow
        expr: node_filesystem_avail_bytes{fstype!=""} / node_filesystem_size_bytes{fstype!=""} * 100 < 10
        for: 5m
        labels:
          severity: critical
        annotations:
          summary: "Low disk space on {{ $labels.instance }}"
          description: "{{ $labels.mountpoint }} has {{ $value }}% free space"
      
      # Network alerts
      - alert: HighNetworkLatency
        expr: probe_duration_seconds > 1
        for: 5m
        labels:
          severity: warning
        annotations:
          summary: "High network latency to {{ $labels.target }}"
          description: "Network latency is {{ $value }}s (threshold 1s)"
      
      - alert: PacketLossDetected
        expr: probe_success == 0
        for: 2m
        labels:
          severity: critical
        annotations:
          summary: "Packet loss detected to {{ $labels.target }}"
          description: "Target {{ $labels.target }} is unreachable"
      
      # Database alerts
      - alert: SlowDatabaseQueries
        expr: rate(pg_stat_database_tup_returned[5m]) > 10000
        for: 10m
        labels:
          severity: warning
        annotations:
          summary: "High rate of slow queries on {{ $labels.datname }}"
          description: "Database {{ $labels.datname }} has high query rate"
      
      - alert: DatabaseConnectionExhaustion
        expr: pg_stat_database_numbackends / (SELECT setting FROM pg_settings WHERE name = 'max_connections') * 100 > 80
        for: 5m
        labels:
          severity: warning
        annotations:
          summary: "Database connection pool nearing exhaustion"
          description: "{{ $value }}% of connections used"
      
      # Thread pool alerts
      - alert: ThreadPoolExhaustion
        expr: jvm_threads_live_threads / jvm_threads_peak > 0.9
        for: 5m
        labels:
          severity: warning
        annotations:
          summary: "Thread pool near capacity on {{ $labels.instance }}"
          description: "{{ $value }}% of peak threads used"
      
      # GC alerts
      - alert: FrequentGarbageCollection
        expr: rate(jvm_gc_pause_seconds_count[5m]) > 10
        for: 10m
        labels:
          severity: warning
        annotations:
          summary: "Frequent GC pauses on {{ $labels.instance }}"
          description: "GC frequency is {{ $value }} per second"
      
      - alert: LongGCPause
        expr: rate(jvm_gc_pause_seconds_sum[5m]) / rate(jvm_gc_pause_seconds_count[5m]) > 1
        for: 5m
        labels:
          severity: critical
        annotations:
          summary: "Long GC pauses on {{ $labels.instance }}"
          description: "Average GC pause time is {{ $value }}s"

content.code:
# scope_analysis.py
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
import requests
import json

class PerformanceScoping:
    def __init__(self, prometheus_url):
        self.prometheus_url = prometheus_url
    
    def query_prometheus(self, query, start_time, end_time):
        """Query Prometheus for metrics"""
        params = {
            'query': query,
            'start': start_time.timestamp(),
            'end': end_time.timestamp(),
            'step': '15s'
        }
        response = requests.get(f"{self.prometheus_url}/api/v1/query_range", params=params)
        return response.json()
    
    def scope_by_time(self, service, duration_hours=24):
        """Analyze performance pattern over time"""
        end_time = datetime.now()
        start_time = end_time - timedelta(hours=duration_hours)
        
        # Query response times
        query = f'histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{{service="{service}"}}[5m])) by (le))'
        result = self.query_prometheus(query, start_time, end_time)
        
        # Process results
        times = []
        values = []
        for sample in result['data']['result'][0]['values']:
            times.append(datetime.fromtimestamp(sample[0]))
            values.append(float(sample[1]))
        
        df = pd.DataFrame({'timestamp': times, 'p95_latency': values})
        
        # Detect change points
        df['hour'] = df['timestamp'].dt.hour
        df['day_of_week'] = df['timestamp'].dt.dayofweek
        
        # Calculate baseline (same hour, previous days)
        baseline = df.groupby('hour')['p95_latency'].transform('median')
        df['deviation'] = (df['p95_latency'] - baseline) / baseline * 100
        
        # Identify significant deviations
        anomalies = df[df['deviation'] > 50]  # >50% deviation
        
        return {
            'service': service,
            'period_analyzed': f"{start_time} to {end_time}",
            'current_p95': df['p95_latency'].iloc[-1],
            'baseline_p95': baseline.iloc[-1],
            'current_deviation': df['deviation'].iloc[-1],
            'anomaly_count': len(anomalies),
            'anomaly_times': anomalies['timestamp'].tolist(),
            'peak_time': df.loc[df['p95_latency'].idxmax(), 'timestamp'],
            'peak_value': df['p95_latency'].max()
        }
    
    def scope_by_endpoint(self, service, window_minutes=60):
        """Identify which endpoints are slow"""
        end_time = datetime.now()
        start_time = end_time - timedelta(minutes=window_minutes)

            if values:
                endpoints.append({

                    'avg_latency': np.mean(values),
                    'max_latency': np.max(values),
                    'min_latency': np.min(values),
                    'current': values[-1]
                })
        
        # Sort by current latency

        perf_result = self.query_prometheus(perf_query, start_time, end_time)
        
        # Create timeline

        for sample in perf_result['data']['result'][0]['values']:
            timeline.append({

                'value': float(sample[1])
            })
        
        # Mark deployments
        for dep in deployments:
            dep_time = datetime.fromisoformat(dep['timestamp'])
            # Find nearest performance data point
            for point in timeline:
                if abs((point['timestamp'] - dep_time).total_seconds()) < 3600:
                    point['deployment'] = dep['version']
                    point['deployment_type'] = dep['type']
        
        return timeline
    
    def generate_scoping_report(self, service):

        print(f"{'='*60}")

        # Endpoint analysis

        if endpoints and endpoints[0]['current'] > 2:

        if time_scope['anomaly_count'] > 10:
            print("• Multiple anomalies detected - check for pattern")
        
        return time_scope, endpoints

# Example usage

#!/bin/bash
# thread_dump_analysis.sh

# Script to analyze thread dumps and identify contention

if [ $# -eq 0 ]; then
    echo "Usage: $0 <thread-dump-file>"
    exit 1
fi

THREAD_DUMP=$1

echo "===== THREAD DUMP ANALYSIS ====="
echo "File: $THREAD_DUMP"
echo ""

# Count total threads
TOTAL_THREADS=$(grep -c '"\?[A-Za-z0-9_-]\+"\? #' "$THREAD_DUMP")
echo "Total threads: $TOTAL_THREADS"

# Count threads by state
echo ""
echo "Thread States:"
grep -o 'java.lang.Thread.State: [A-Z_]\+' "$THREAD_DUMP" | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr

# Find blocked threads
echo ""
echo "BLOCKED threads (potential contention):"
BLOCKED=$(grep -B 5 'java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED' "$THREAD_DUMP" | grep '"\?[A-Za-z0-9_-]\+"\? #' | sed 's/^"\(.*\)".*/\1/')
if [ -n "$BLOCKED" ]; then
    echo "$BLOCKED" | nl
else
    echo "None found"
fi

# Find threads waiting for locks
echo ""
echo "Threads waiting for locks:"
grep -B 2 'waiting to lock' "$THREAD_DUMP" | grep '"\?[A-Za-z0-9_-]\+"\? #' | sed 's/^"\(.*\)".*/\1/' | nl

# Find deadlocks
echo ""
echo "DEADLOCK detection:"
DEADLOCK=$(grep -A 10 -i 'deadlock' "$THREAD_DUMP")
if [ -n "$DEADLOCK" ]; then
    echo "⚠️ DEADLOCK FOUND!"
    echo "$DEADLOCK"
else
    echo "No deadlocks detected"
fi

# Most frequent stack traces (top 10)
echo ""
echo "Top 10 most frequent stack trace patterns:"
grep 'at ' "$THREAD_DUMP" | sed 's/at //' | sed 's/(.*)//' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -10

# CPU usage estimation (based on RUNNABLE threads)
echo ""
echo "CPU Usage Estimation:"
RUNNABLE=$(grep -c 'java.lang.Thread.State: RUNNABLE' "$THREAD_DUMP")
echo "Runnable threads: $RUNNABLE (potential CPU consumers)"
if [ $RUNNABLE -gt $(($TOTAL_THREADS / 2)) ]; then
    echo "⚠️ High number of runnable threads - possible CPU bottleneck"
fi

# Analyze lock contention
echo ""
echo "Lock Contention Analysis:"
echo "Most contended locks:"
grep -o '\<0x[0-9a-f]\+\>' "$THREAD_DUMP" | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -10

# Generate summary
echo ""
echo "===== SUMMARY ====="
if [ -n "$DEADLOCK" ]; then
    echo "❌ CRITICAL: Deadlock detected!"
elif [ $(grep -c 'java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED' "$THREAD_DUMP") -gt 10 ]; then
    echo "⚠️ WARNING: High thread contention (>10 blocked threads)"
else
    echo "✅ No critical issues detected"
fi

# Suggest next steps
echo ""
echo "Recommended actions:"
if [ $(grep -c 'java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED' "$THREAD_DUMP") -gt 0 ]; then
    echo "• Investigate BLOCKED threads - check synchronized blocks and locks"
fi
if [ $RUNNABLE -gt $(($TOTAL_THREADS * 8 / 10)) ]; then
    echo "• High Runnable count - profile CPU usage to find hot methods"
fi
if [ $(grep -c 'java.lang.Thread.State: TIMED_WAITING' "$THREAD_DUMP") -gt $(($TOTAL_THREADS / 2)) ]; then
    echo "• Many TIMED_WAITING threads - check connection pools and timeouts"
fi

# hypothesis_testing.py
import requests
import time
import statistics
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
import argparse
import json
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed

class PerformanceHypothesisTester:
    def __init__(self, base_url, endpoint):
        self.base_url = base_url
        self.endpoint = endpoint
        self.results = []
    
    def run_test(self, config, num_requests=100, concurrency=10):
        """Run performance test with specific configuration"""
        print(f"\n🔬 Testing hypothesis: {config['name']}")
        print(f"Configuration: {config['description']}")
        
        latencies = []
        errors = 0
        
        with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=concurrency) as executor:
            futures = []
            for i in range(num_requests):
                futures.append(
                    executor.submit(self._make_request, config)
                )
            
            for future in as_completed(futures):
                success, latency = future.result()
                if success:
                    latencies.append(latency)
                else:
                    errors += 1
        
        # Calculate statistics
        result = {
            'config_name': config['name'],
            'num_requests': num_requests,
            'successful_requests': len(latencies),
            'errors': errors,
            'error_rate': errors / num_requests * 100,
            'latencies': latencies,
            'mean_latency': statistics.mean(latencies) if latencies else None,
            'median_latency': statistics.median(latencies) if latencies else None,
            'p95_latency': np.percentile(latencies, 95) if latencies else None,
            'p99_latency': np.percentile(latencies, 99) if latencies else None,
            'std_dev': statistics.stdev(latencies) if len(latencies) > 1 else None
        }
        
        self.results.append(result)
        self._print_result(result)
        return result
    
    def _make_request(self, config):
        """Make single request with config"""
        url = f"{self.base_url}{self.endpoint}"
        headers = config.get('headers', {})
        params = config.get('params', {})
        
        try:
            start = time.time()
            response = requests.get(url, headers=headers, params=params, timeout=10)
            latency = (time.time() - start) * 1000  # ms
            
            if response.status_code == 200:
                return True, latency
            else:
                return False, latency
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"Request error: {e}")
            return False, None
    
    def _print_result(self, result):
        print(f"\n📊 Results for {result['config_name']}:")
        print(f"  Successful requests: {result['successful_requests']}/{result['num_requests']}")
        print(f"  Error rate: {result['error_rate']:.2f}%")
        if result['mean_latency']:
            print(f"  Mean latency: {result['mean_latency']:.2f} ms")
            print(f"  Median latency: {result['median_latency']:.2f} ms")
            print(f"  p95 latency: {result['p95_latency']:.2f} ms")
            print(f"  p99 latency: {result['p99_latency']:.2f} ms")
    
    def compare_hypotheses(self):
        """Compare results from different hypotheses"""
        if len(self.results) < 2:
            print("Need at least two test runs to compare")
            return
        
        print("\n🔍 HYPOTHESIS COMPARISON")
        print("=" * 60)
        
        baseline = self.results[0]
        for i, result in enumerate(self.results[1:], 1):
            print(f"\nComparing {result['config_name']} vs {baseline['config_name']}:")
            
            # Statistical significance test (Mann-Whitney U test)
            if result['latencies'] and baseline['latencies']:
                stat, p_value = stats.mannwhitneyu(
                    result['latencies'], 
                    baseline['latencies'], 
                    alternative='two-sided'
                )
                
                print(f"  Mann-Whitney U test p-value: {p_value:.4f}")
                if p_value < 0.05:
                    print("  ✅ Statistically significant difference (p < 0.05)")
                else:
                    print("  ❌ No statistically significant difference")
                
                # Improvement percentage
                improvement = (baseline['mean_latency'] - result['mean_latency']) / baseline['mean_latency'] * 100
                print(f"  Mean latency change: {improvement:+.1f}%")
                
                if result['error_rate'] < baseline['error_rate']:
                    print(f"  Error rate improved: {baseline['error_rate']:.2f}% → {result['error_rate']:.2f}%")
                else:
                    print(f"  Error rate worsened: {baseline['error_rate']:.2f}% → {result['error_rate']:.2f}%")
    
    def export_results(self, filename):
        """Export results to JSON"""
        export_data = {
            'test_config': {
                'base_url': self.base_url,
                'endpoint': self.endpoint,
            },
            'results': self.results
        }
        with open(filename, 'w') as f:
            json.dump(export_data, f, indent=2, default=str)
        print(f"\n💾 Results exported to {filename}")

# Example usage
def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description='Test performance hypotheses')
    parser.add_argument('--url', required=True, help='Base URL')
    parser.add_argument('--endpoint', default='/api/test', help='Endpoint to test')
    parser.add_argument('--requests', type=int, default=100, help='Number of requests')
    parser.add_argument('--concurrency', type=int, default=10, help='Concurrent requests')
    args = parser.parse_args()
    
    tester = PerformanceHypothesisTester(args.url, args.endpoint)
    
    # Hypothesis 1: Baseline (no changes)
    tester.run_test({
        'name': 'Baseline',
        'description': 'Current production configuration',
        'headers': {},
        'params': {}
    }, num_requests=args.requests, concurrency=args.concurrency)
    
    # Hypothesis 2: Add caching headers
    tester.run_test({
        'name': 'With Caching Headers',
        'description': 'Added Cache-Control: max-age=60',
        'headers': {'Cache-Control': 'max-age=60'},
        'params': {}
    }, num_requests=args.requests, concurrency=args.concurrency)
    
    # Hypothesis 3: Connection pooling
    tester.run_test({
        'name': 'Keep-Alive Enabled',
        'description': 'Using HTTP keep-alive connections',
        'headers': {'Connection': 'keep-alive'},
        'params': {}
    }, num_requests=args.requests, concurrency=args.concurrency)
    
    # Compare results
    tester.compare_hypotheses()
    
    # Export
    tester.export_results('hypothesis_test_results.json')

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

content.value: Before implementing a fix, you must validate that you've truly found the root cause. This step prevents wasted effort on symptoms rather than the actual problem.

content.title: Validation Checklist
items: ✅ **Reproduce consistently** – Can you make the bottleneck appear on demand?
✅ **Isolate completely** – Can you eliminate all other variables?
✅ **Measure impact** – What percentage of total time does this account for?
✅ **Correlate with symptoms** – Does fixing this component eliminate the observed symptoms?
✅ **Test in isolation** – Can you demonstrate the bottleneck in a minimal test environment?
✅ **Consider alternatives** – Could something else cause the same symptoms?
✅ **Document evidence** – Collect metrics, traces, logs that prove causation

# root_cause_validation.py
import time
import psutil
import subprocess
import json
from datetime import datetime

class RootCauseValidator:
    def __init__(self, service_name):
        self.service_name = service_name
        self.evidence = []
    
    def collect_before_metrics(self):
        """Collect metrics before applying fix"""
        print("📊 Collecting baseline metrics...")
        metrics = {
            'timestamp': datetime.now().isoformat(),
            'cpu_percent': psutil.cpu_percent(interval=1, percpu=True),
            'memory_percent': psutil.virtual_memory().percent,
            'disk_io': psutil.disk_io_counters()._asdict() if psutil.disk_io_counters() else {},
            'net_io': psutil.net_io_counters()._asdict(),
            'connections': len(psutil.net_connections())
        }
        
        # Get process-specific metrics if available
        for proc in psutil.process_iter(['pid', 'name', 'cpu_percent', 'memory_percent']):
            if self.service_name in proc.info['name']:
                metrics['process'] = proc.info
                break
        
        return metrics
    
    def collect_after_metrics(self):
        """Collect metrics after applying fix"""
        print("📊 Collecting post-fix metrics...")
        time.sleep(2)  # Allow system to stabilize
        return self.collect_before_metrics()  # Reuse the same collection
    
    def run_validation_test(self, test_command, expected_improvement=20):
        """Run a validation test to confirm the fix"""
        print(f"\n🔬 Running validation test: {test_command}")
        
        # Run test before fix
        print("\n⏱️  Testing BEFORE fix...")
        before_metrics = self.collect_before_metrics()
        
        before_result = subprocess.run(
            test_command,
            shell=True,
            capture_output=True,
            text=True
        )
        
        # Parse before result (assuming the command outputs time in ms)
        try:
            before_time = float(before_result.stdout.strip())
        except:
            before_time = None
        
        # Apply fix (simulated - in real scenario you'd deploy the fix)
        print("\n🔧 Applying fix...")
        self.apply_fix()
        time.sleep(5)  # Wait for fix to take effect
        
        # Run test after fix
        print("\n⏱️  Testing AFTER fix...")
        after_metrics = self.collect_after_metrics()
        
        after_result = subprocess.run(
            test_command,
            shell=True,
            capture_output=True,
            text=True
        )
        
        try:
            after_time = float(after_result.stdout.strip())
        except:
            after_time = None
        
        # Calculate improvement
        if before_time and after_time:
            improvement = ((before_time - after_time) / before_time) * 100
            print(f"\n📈 Improvement: {improvement:.1f}%")
            
            # Validate against expected improvement
            if improvement >= expected_improvement:
                print(f"✅ Validation PASSED: Improvement meets/exceeds {expected_improvement}%")
                self.evidence.append({
                    'test': test_command,
                    'before': before_time,
                    'after': after_time,
                    'improvement': improvement,
                    'status': 'PASS'
                })
            else:
                print(f"❌ Validation FAILED: Improvement below expected {expected_improvement}%")
                self.evidence.append({
                    'test': test_command,
                    'before': before_time,
                    'after': after_time,
                    'improvement': improvement,
                    'status': 'FAIL'
                })
        
        # Compare metrics
        self.compare_metrics(before_metrics, after_metrics)
        
        return improvement if before_time and after_time else None
    
    def apply_fix(self):
        """Apply the fix (placeholder - customize for your environment)"""
        # In a real scenario, this might:
        # - Deploy new code
        # - Change configuration
        # - Add an index
        # - Scale resources
        print("   Fix applied (simulated)")
    
    def compare_metrics(self, before, after):
        """Compare metrics before and after fix"""
        print("\n📊 Metric Comparison:")
        
        # CPU comparison
        before_cpu_avg = sum(before['cpu_percent']) / len(before['cpu_percent'])
        after_cpu_avg = sum(after['cpu_percent']) / len(after['cpu_percent'])
        cpu_change = ((before_cpu_avg - after_cpu_avg) / before_cpu_avg) * 100
        print(f"  CPU: {before_cpu_avg:.1f}% → {after_cpu_avg:.1f}% ({cpu_change:+.1f}%)")
        
        # Memory comparison
        memory_change = before['memory_percent'] - after['memory_percent']
        print(f"  Memory: {before['memory_percent']:.1f}% → {after['memory_percent']:.1f}% ({memory_change:+.1f}%)")
        
        # Connections
        conn_change = before['connections'] - after['connections']
        print(f"  Connections: {before['connections']} → {after['connections']} ({conn_change:+d})")
    
    def generate_validation_report(self):
        """Generate comprehensive validation report"""
        report = {
            'service': self.service_name,
            'validation_time': datetime.now().isoformat(),
            'evidence': self.evidence,
            'overall_status': 'PASS' if all(e['status'] == 'PASS' for e in self.evidence) else 'FAIL'
        }
        
        # Save to file
        filename = f"validation_report_{datetime.now().strftime('%Y%m%d_%H%M%S')}.json"
        with open(filename, 'w') as f:
            json.dump(report, f, indent=2)
        
        print(f"\n📄 Validation report saved to {filename}")
        return report

# Example usage
if __name__ == "__main__":
    validator = RootCauseValidator("payment-service")
    
    # Run validation test
    improvement = validator.run_validation_test(
        "curl -o /dev/null -s -w '%{time_total}\n' http://localhost:8080/api/payment/123",
        expected_improvement=30
    )
    
    # Generate report
    validator.generate_validation_report()

content.value: Systematic methodology transforms performance troubleshooting from guesswork to science. Detection alerts you to problems. Scoping defines the boundaries. Drill-down analysis investigates each layer. Hypothesis testing isolates the root cause. Validation confirms you've found the real issue. This approach ensures you fix the right problem and can prove it. In the next section, we'll explore real-world case studies applying this methodology.

Theory is essential, but real learning comes from seeing how bottlenecks manifest and get resolved in actual systems. This section presents detailed case studies across different technologies and scenarios.

content.title: 5.1 Case Study: Database Connection Pool Exhaustion

content.value: **The Scenario:** A popular e-commerce site experiences intermittent slowdowns during peak shopping hours. Response times spike from 200ms to 5+ seconds for 10-15 minutes, then recover. The pattern is unpredictable but happens 2-3 times per day.

items.definition:
• Response time spikes to 5+ seconds
• Error rate increases during spikes
• Some requests timeout completely
• Database CPU remains moderate (40-60%)
• Application CPU also moderate

• Affects all API endpoints that touch the database
• Correlates with high traffic periods but not every time
• Pattern suggests resource exhaustion rather than query slowdown
• Database metrics show normal query times when queries execute

• Checked database connection pool metrics
• Found connection pool reaching max size during spikes
• Active connections max out at 50 (pool limit)
• Many requests waiting for connections (queue depth spikes)
• Connection acquisition time increases from 2ms to 3+ seconds

• Connection pool size too small for peak load
• Some transactions hold connections longer than expected due to slow external API calls within transactions
• Connection leak in one service (connections not released in finally block)
• No connection timeout configured for stuck transactions

• Increased connection pool from 50 to 100
• Added connection timeout (30 seconds)
• Fixed connection leak with try-with-resources
• Moved external API calls outside transactions
• Added connection pool monitoring with alerts at 80% usage

content.caption: Fixed Connection Pool Configuration

content.title: Active Connections After Fix
content.caption: After fix: Connections scale with load without hitting the pool limit.

content.title: 5.2 Case Study: Memory Leak in Java Application

content.value: **The Scenario:** A document processing service runs fine for a few hours after deployment, then gradually slows down until it becomes completely unresponsive. Restarting the service temporarily fixes it, but the problem returns.

items.definition:
• Service slows down over time (hours)
• Response time gradually increases from 100ms to 10+ seconds
• Eventually, service stops responding entirely
• Restart provides temporary relief (hours)
• Memory usage graph shows steady increase until near limit

• Only affects this specific service
• Pattern consistent with memory leak
• GC logs show increasing GC frequency and duration
• Eventually, GC overhead limit exceeded errors
• Heap dumps show certain object types accumulating

• Captured heap dumps at regular intervals
• Used Eclipse MAT to analyze object retention
• Found thousands of Document objects still referenced
• Document objects held by a cache that never expires
• Cache entries added but never removed

• In-memory cache of processed documents
• Cache size unbounded (no eviction policy)
• Documents retained forever once cached
• Each document ~5MB, cache grows until heap exhausted
• No weak references or size limits

• Implemented LRU eviction policy
• Set maximum cache size (100 documents)
• Used weak references for cache keys
• Added cache statistics monitoring
• Implemented scheduled cache cleanup

content.caption: Fixed Cache Implementation with Eviction

content.value: **The Scenario:** A content management API that returns articles with their authors and comments is fast during development but slows down dramatically in production with real data. Response time for a list of 20 articles is over 5 seconds.

items.definition:
• API endpoint /api/articles returns 20 articles
• Response time ~5 seconds
• Database CPU spikes during request
• Number of database queries = 1 (for articles) + 20 (for authors) + 20*comments (40) = 61 queries
• Each query fast (2-5ms), but 61 queries = 300ms network + overhead

• Problem isolated to this specific endpoint
• Database shows many small queries from same connection
• Hibernate statistics show 61 queries for single request
• SQL log confirms N+1 pattern

• JPA entity mappings use FetchType.LAZY but accessed in loop
• Each article.getAuthor() triggers separate query
• Each article.getComments().size() triggers separate query
• No JOIN FETCH in JPQL query

• Classic N+1 query problem
• ORM lazy loading causes multiple queries in loop
• Network overhead dominates (61 round trips)
• Database connection not the issue; query count is

• Changed query to use JOIN FETCH for authors
• Used batch fetching for comments
• Added @BatchSize annotation
• Implemented entity graphs for fine-grained control
• Added query logging to detect N+1 in development

content.caption: Fixing N+1 Queries in JPA

content.title: 5.4 Case Study: CPU Saturation from Inefficient JSON Processing

content.value: **The Scenario:** A data processing service that receives large JSON payloads (up to 10MB) starts experiencing high CPU usage and slow response times as traffic increases. The service parses JSON, validates, and stores in database.

items.definition:
• CPU consistently at 90-100%
• Response time increases with payload size
• Throughput plateaus at 50 requests/second
• Memory usage normal
• Database not a bottleneck

• Only affects this service
• CPU usage correlates with request rate

Memory leaks require heap analysis and proper cache management. N+1 queries highlight ORM pitfalls. JSON processing inefficiency demonstrates the value of profiling and targeted optimization. Each case followed the methodology: detect, scope, analyze, isolate, validate.

Once you've identified a bottleneck, you need effective strategies to fix it. This section catalogs optimization techniques for each bottleneck type, from quick configuration changes to fundamental architectural redesign.

items.definition: Add indexes for WHERE clauses, JOIN conditions, and ORDER BY. Use composite indexes for multi-column queries. Consider covering indexes to include all needed columns. Monitor index usage and remove unused indexes.

Rewrite N+1 queries as JOINs. Use EXISTS instead of IN for large subqueries. Avoid SELECT *. Use UNION ALL instead of UNION when possible. Optimize pagination with keyset pagination (WHERE id > last_id) instead of OFFSET.
Size pool appropriately (connections = ((core_count * 2) + effective_spindle_count)). Set timeouts to prevent hung connections. Monitor pool usage and add alerts. Use connection validation queries.
Implement query result caching. Use Redis/Memcached for frequently accessed data. Consider application-level caching for reference data. Use database query cache appropriately.
Normalize for writes, denormalize for reads. Use appropriate data types (INT vs BIGINT, VARCHAR vs TEXT). Partition large tables. Archive old data. Consider read replicas for reporting queries.
Adjust buffer sizes (innodb_buffer_pool_size for MySQL, shared_buffers for PostgreSQL). Tune checkpoint intervals. Optimize WAL/log settings. Adjust sort/memory limits for queries.

-- database_optimizations.sql

-- ===== INDEX OPTIMIZATION =====

-- Find missing indexes (simplified - use pt-query-digest for production)
SELECT 
    CONCAT(table_schema, '.', table_name) as table_name,
    seq_in_index,
    column_name,
    cardinality,
    (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM information_schema.statistics s2 
     WHERE s2.table_schema = s.table_schema 
     AND s2.table_name = s.table_name) as total_indexes
FROM information_schema.statistics s
WHERE table_schema NOT IN ('mysql', 'information_schema', 'performance_schema')
AND seq_in_index = 1
ORDER BY cardinality ASC
LIMIT 20;

-- Create composite index for common query pattern
-- Query: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ? AND created_at > ? ORDER BY created_at DESC
CREATE INDEX idx_customer_created ON orders(customer_id, created_at DESC);

-- Covering index (includes all needed columns)
-- Query: SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ?
CREATE INDEX idx_customer_covering ON orders(customer_id) INCLUDE (status, total);

-- Partial index (PostgreSQL) - only index active orders
CREATE INDEX idx_active_orders ON orders(created_at) WHERE status = 'active';

-- ===== QUERY REWRITES =====

-- Bad: SELECT * with large offset
SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY id LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10000;

-- Good: Keyset pagination (remember last ID from previous page)
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id > 10000 ORDER BY id LIMIT 10;

-- Bad: N+1 in application (1 query for parent + N for children)
-- Instead, use JOIN:
SELECT o.*, c.*, i.*
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN customers c ON o.customer_id = c.id
LEFT JOIN order_items i ON o.id = i.order_id
WHERE o.created_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '1 day';

-- Bad: IN with subquery that returns many rows
SELECT * FROM products 
WHERE category_id IN (SELECT id FROM categories WHERE active = true);

-- Good: EXISTS (often faster)
SELECT p.*
FROM products p
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM categories c WHERE c.id = p.category_id AND c.active = true);

-- Bad: Multiple OR conditions
SELECT * FROM orders 
WHERE status = 'pending' OR status = 'processing' OR priority = 'high';

-- Good: UNION (can use different indexes)
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status IN ('pending', 'processing')
UNION
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE priority = 'high' AND status NOT IN ('pending', 'processing');

-- ===== CONNECTION POOLING (application side - HikariCP example) =====
-- In application.properties
-- spring.datasource.hikari.maximumPoolSize=50
-- spring.datasource.hikari.minimumIdle=10
-- spring.datasource.hikari.connectionTimeout=30000
-- spring.datasource.hikari.idleTimeout=600000
-- spring.datasource.hikari.maxLifetime=1800000
-- spring.datasource.hikari.leakDetectionThreshold=10000

-- ===== DATABASE CONFIGURATION TUNING =====

-- PostgreSQL tuning (postgresql.conf)
-- shared_buffers = 4GB (25% of RAM if dedicated)
-- work_mem = 32MB (per operation)
-- maintenance_work_mem = 512MB
-- effective_cache_size = 12GB (50-75% of RAM)
-- wal_buffers = 16MB
-- checkpoint_completion_target = 0.9
-- random_page_cost = 1.1 (for SSD)
-- max_connections = 200

-- MySQL/InnoDB tuning (my.cnf)
-- innodb_buffer_pool_size = 8G (70-80% of RAM)
-- innodb_log_file_size = 2G
-- innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit = 2 (better performance, slightly less durable)
-- innodb_flush_method = O_DIRECT
-- query_cache_type = 0 (disable, usually harmful in modern MySQL)
-- max_connections = 500

-- ===== CACHING STRATEGIES =====

-- Application-level caching with Redis (pseudo-code)
/*
public Product getProduct(Long id) {
    // Try cache first
    String cached = redis.get("product:" + id);
    if (cached != null) {
        return jsonToProduct(cached);
    }
    
    // Cache miss - query database
    Product product = productRepository.findById(id);
    
    // Store in cache with expiration
    redis.setex("product:" + id, 3600, productToJson(product));
    
    return product;
}
*/

-- ===== READ REPLICAS =====
-- Route read-only queries to replicas
-- In application, use @Transactional(readOnly = true) to route to replica

-- ===== TABLE PARTITIONING =====

-- PostgreSQL range partitioning
CREATE TABLE orders_2024 PARTITION OF orders
FOR VALUES FROM ('2024-01-01') TO ('2025-01-01');

-- MySQL partitioning
ALTER TABLE orders PARTITION BY RANGE (YEAR(created_at)) (
    PARTITION p2022 VALUES LESS THAN (2023),
    PARTITION p2023 VALUES LESS THAN (2024),
    PARTITION p2024 VALUES LESS THAN (2025),
    PARTITION future VALUES LESS THAN MAXVALUE
);

items.definition: Replace O(n²) algorithms with O(n log n) or O(n). Use appropriate data structures (HashMap for lookups, ArrayList for iteration). Cache expensive computations. Lazy load where appropriate.
Reduce lock scope. Use concurrent collections (ConcurrentHashMap). Consider optimistic locking. Use thread pools appropriately. Avoid synchronization where not needed. Use atomic variables.
Use buffered I/O. Batch database operations. Use asynchronous I/O for non-blocking operations. Compress large responses. Use connection pooling for all external services.
Avoid creating unnecessary objects. Use primitive types where possible. Pool expensive objects. Use weak references for caches. Tune GC settings. Watch for memory leaks.
Implement pagination for list endpoints. Support partial responses (fields filtering). Use compression (gzip). Implement ETags for caching. Consider GraphQL for complex data needs.
Cache at multiple levels (CDN, application, database). Use cache-aside or read-through patterns. Set appropriate TTLs. Invalidate cache on updates. Consider distributed caches.

items.definition: Increase resources (CPU, RAM, disk) on existing instances. Often the simplest fix but has limits. Consider when bottleneck is resource exhaustion and workload isn't easily distributed.
Add more instances behind load balancer. Requires stateless applications or distributed session management. Effective for CPU-bound, memory-bound, and many I/O workloads.
Read replicas for read-heavy workloads. Database sharding for write-heavy. Connection pooling. Caching layer (Redis/Memcached). Consider NewSQL for extreme scale.
CDN for static assets. Reverse proxy caching (Varnish, Nginx). Distributed cache (Redis cluster). Application cache. Database query cache.
Distribute traffic across instances. Health checks to remove unhealthy instances. Sticky sessions if needed (but prefer stateless). Layer 7 routing for API gateways.
Scale based on metrics (CPU, memory, request rate). Predictive scaling for known patterns. Scale down during low traffic to save costs. Container orchestration (Kubernetes).

    limit_req_zone $binary_remote_addr zone=api_limit:10m rate=100r/s;

content.title: Introducing Failure to Find Weaknesses
content.explanation:
Chaos engineering involves intentionally injecting failures to see how the system behaves. For performance, this means introducing latency, throttling resources, or killing instances to find resilience and performance boundaries.

**Key Experiments:**
- **Latency Injection** – Add delays to database calls to test timeout handling
- **Resource Throttling** – Limit CPU/memory to simulate resource contention
- **Instance Termination** – Kill instances to test load balancer failover
- **Network Degradation** – Simulate packet loss or bandwidth limits
- **Dependency Failure** – Make external services return errors

**Principles:**
- Start with small blast radius
- Have monitoring in place
- Know your steady state
- Automate experiments
- Learn and fix

content.caption: Chaos Engineering Experiments for Performance
content.code:
# chaos_experiments.py
import random
import time
import requests
import threading
import subprocess
from datetime import datetime

class ChaosExperiment:
    def __init__(self, service_name, base_url):
        self.service_name = service_name
        self.base_url = base_url
        self.running = False
        self.metrics = []
    
    def inject_latency(self, target, latency_ms=1000, duration_sec=30):
        """Inject latency into network calls using tc (traffic control)"""
        print(f"[CHAOS] Injecting {latency_ms}ms latency to {target} for {duration_sec}s")
        
        # Using tc on Linux to add network latency
        cmd = f"tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem delay {latency_ms}ms"
        
        try:
            # Start latency injection
            subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True, check=True)
            
            # Measure impact
            start_time = time.time()
            while time.time() - start_time < duration_sec:
                self.measure_response_time()
                time.sleep(1)
        finally:
            # Remove latency
            subprocess.run("tc qdisc del dev eth0 root netem", shell=True)
        
        print("[CHAOS] Latency injection completed")
    
    def throttle_cpu(self, cpu_percent=50, duration_sec=60):
        """Throttle CPU using cpulimit"""
        print(f"[CHAOS] Throttling CPU to {cpu_percent}% for {duration_sec}s")
        
        # Get PID of service
        pid_cmd = f"pgrep -f {self.service_name}"
        result = subprocess.run(pid_cmd, shell=True, capture_output=True, text=True)
        pid = result.stdout.strip()
        
        if not pid:
            print(f"[CHAOS] Could not find process for {self.service_name}")
            return
        
        # Start cpulimit
        cpulimit_cmd = f"cpulimit -p {pid} -l {cpu_percent} -b"
        subprocess.run(cpulimit_cmd, shell=True)
        
        # Monitor during throttling
        start_time = time.time()
        while time.time() - start_time < duration_sec:
            self.measure_response_time()
            time.sleep(2)
        
        # Kill cpulimit
        subprocess.run("pkill cpulimit", shell=True)
        print("[CHAOS] CPU throttling completed")
    
    def kill_instance(self, instance_id):
        """Kill a service instance to test failover"""
        print(f"[CHAOS] Killing instance {instance_id}")
        
        # Simulate instance failure
        # In real environment, this might terminate an EC2 instance or kill a container
        
        # Measure before
        before_metrics = self.measure_response_time(10)
        
        # Kill instance (simulated here with process kill)
        kill_cmd = f"docker kill {instance_id}"  # or kubectl delete pod
        subprocess.run(kill_cmd, shell=True)
        
        # Measure during recovery
        time.sleep(5)  # Wait for load balancer to detect failure
        during_metrics = self.measure_response_time(10)
        
        # Wait for auto-scaling to replace
        time.sleep(30)
        after_metrics = self.measure_response_time(10)
        
        print(f"[CHAOS] Before kill: avg={before_metrics['avg_latency']:.2f}ms, errors={before_metrics['errors']}")
        print(f"[CHAOS] During kill: avg={during_metrics['avg_latency']:.2f}ms, errors={during_metrics['errors']}")
        print(f"[CHAOS] After recovery: avg={after_metrics['avg_latency']:.2f}ms, errors={after_metrics['errors']}")
    
    def simulate_packet_loss(self, loss_percent=5, duration_sec=30):
        """Simulate network packet loss"""
        print(f"[CHAOS] Simulating {loss_percent}% packet loss for {duration_sec}s")
        
        cmd = f"tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem loss {loss_percent}%"
        
        try:
            subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True, check=True)
            self.measure_response_time(duration_sec)
        finally:
            subprocess.run("tc qdisc del dev eth0 root netem", shell=True)
    
    def fail_dependency(self, dependency_url, duration_sec=30):
        """Make a dependency return errors"""
        print(f"[CHAOS] Failing dependency {dependency_url} for {duration_sec}s")
        
        # This might involve:
        # - Blocking IP in firewall
        # - Configuring proxy to return 503
        # - Modifying DNS to point to blackhole
        
        # Example using iptables to block traffic
        block_cmd = f"iptables -A OUTPUT -d {dependency_url} -j DROP"
        
        try:
            subprocess.run(block_cmd, shell=True, check=True)
            self.measure_response_time(duration_sec)
        finally:
            subprocess.run(f"iptables -D OUTPUT -d {dependency_url} -j DROP", shell=True)
    
    def measure_response_time(self, duration_sec=10):
        """Measure response times during chaos"""
        latencies = []
        errors = 0
        
        end_time = time.time() + duration_sec
        while time.time() < end_time:
            try:
                start = time.time()
                response = requests.get(f"{self.base_url}/health", timeout=5)
                latency = (time.time() - start) * 1000
                
                if response.status_code == 200:
                    latencies.append(latency)
                else:
                    errors += 1
            except Exception:
                errors += 1
            
            time.sleep(0.5)
        
        metrics = {
            'timestamp': datetime.now().isoformat(),
            'avg_latency': sum(latencies) / len(latencies) if latencies else 0,
            'max_latency': max(latencies) if latencies else 0,
            'min_latency': min(latencies) if latencies else 0,
            'errors': errors,
            'total_requests': len(latencies) + errors
        }
        
        self.metrics.append(metrics)
        return metrics
    
    def run_experiment_suite(self):
        """Run a series of chaos experiments"""
        experiments = [
            (self.inject_latency, {'latency_ms': 500, 'duration_sec': 30}),
            (self.inject_latency, {'latency_ms': 2000, 'duration_sec': 30}),
            (self.throttle_cpu, {'cpu_percent': 30, 'duration_sec': 60}),
            (self.throttle_cpu, {'cpu_percent': 70, 'duration_sec': 60}),
            (self.simulate_packet_loss, {'loss_percent': 2, 'duration_sec': 30}),
            (self.simulate_packet_loss, {'loss_percent': 10, 'duration_sec': 30}),
        ]
        
        results = []
        for experiment, params in experiments:
            print(f"\n{'='*60}")
            print(f"Running experiment: {experiment.__name__}")
            experiment(**params)
            results.append({
                'experiment': experiment.__name__,
                'params': params,
                'metrics': self.metrics[-3:]  # Last 3 measurements
            })
        
        self.generate_report(results)
    
    def generate_report(self, results):
        """Generate chaos experiment report"""
        print("\n" + "="*60)
        print("CHAOS EXPERIMENT REPORT")
        print("="*60)
        
        for result in results:
            print(f"\nExperiment: {result['experiment']}")
            print(f"Parameters: {result['params']}")
            for i, metrics in enumerate(result['metrics']):
                print(f"  Phase {i+1}: avg={metrics['avg_latency']:.2f}ms, errors={metrics['errors']}")

# Example usage
if __name__ == "__main__":
    chaos = ChaosExperiment("payment-service", "http://localhost:8080")
    
    # Run individual experiment
    chaos.inject_latency("database.example.com", latency_ms=1000, duration_sec=30)
    
    # Or run suite
    # chaos.run_experiment_suite()

# capacity_planning.py
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')

class CapacityPlanner:
    def __init__(self, historical_data):
        """
        historical_data: DataFrame with columns:
            - timestamp
            - requests_per_second
            - cpu_usage
            - memory_usage
            - response_time_p95
        """
        self.data = historical_data
        self.models = {}
    
    def forecast_traffic(self, days_ahead=90):
        """Forecast future traffic based on historical trends"""
        # Prepare data
        self.data['days_since_start'] = (self.data['timestamp'] - self.data['timestamp'].min()).dt.days
        X = self.data['days_since_start'].values.reshape(-1, 1)
        y = self.data['requests_per_second'].values
        
        # Try linear, quadratic, and exponential models
        models = {
            'linear': LinearRegression(),
            'quadratic': LinearRegression(),
            'exponential': LinearRegression()
        }
        
        # Quadratic features
        poly = PolynomialFeatures(degree=2)
        X_quad = poly.fit_transform(X)
        
        # Exponential (log transform)
        y_log = np.log(y + 1)  # +1 to handle zeros
        
        # Fit models
        models['linear'].fit(X, y)
        models['quadratic'].fit(X_quad, y)
        models['exponential'].fit(X, y_log)
        
        # Make predictions
        future_days = np.arange(self.data['days_since_start'].max() + 1, 
                                 self.data['days_since_start'].max() + days_ahead + 1)
        
        predictions = pd.DataFrame({
            'days': future_days,
            'linear': models['linear'].predict(future_days.reshape(-1, 1)),
            'quadratic': models['quadratic'].predict(poly.transform(future_days.reshape(-1, 1))),
            'exponential': np.exp(models['exponential'].predict(future_days.reshape(-1, 1))) - 1
        })
        
        # Use the most conservative (highest) prediction for planning
        predictions['conservative'] = predictions[['linear', 'quadratic', 'exponential']].max(axis=1)
        
        self.models['traffic'] = models
        
        return predictions
    
    def predict_resource_needs(self, traffic_forecast):
        """Predict resource requirements based on traffic"""
        # Model relationship between traffic and resource usage
        X = self.data['requests_per_second'].values.reshape(-1, 1)
        y_cpu = self.data['cpu_usage'].values
        y_memory = self.data['memory_usage'].values
        y_response = self.data['response_time_p95'].values
        
        # Fit models
        cpu_model = LinearRegression().fit(X, y_cpu)
        memory_model = LinearRegression().fit(X, y_memory)
        response_model = LinearRegression().fit(X, y_response)
        
        # Predict for future traffic
        future_traffic = traffic_forecast['conservative'].values.reshape(-1, 1)
        
        traffic_forecast['predicted_cpu'] = cpu_model.predict(future_traffic)
        traffic_forecast['predicted_memory'] = memory_model.predict(future_traffic)
        traffic_forecast['predicted_response'] = response_model.predict(future_traffic)
        
        # Add thresholds
        traffic_forecast['cpu_exceeded'] = traffic_forecast['predicted_cpu'] > 80
        traffic_forecast['memory_exceeded'] = traffic_forecast['predicted_memory'] > 80
        traffic_forecast['response_exceeded'] = traffic_forecast['predicted_response'] > 1000  # 1s
        
        return traffic_forecast
    
    def find_saturation_points(self, forecast):
        """Find when resources will saturate"""
        saturation = {}
        
        # Find first day each metric exceeds threshold
        cpu_saturation = forecast[forecast['predicted_cpu'] > 80]
        if not cpu_saturation.empty:
            saturation['cpu'] = {
                'day': cpu_saturation.iloc[0]['days'],
                'traffic': cpu_saturation.iloc[0]['conservative'],
                'value': cpu_saturation.iloc[0]['predicted_cpu']
            }
        
        memory_saturation = forecast[forecast['predicted_memory'] > 80]
        if not memory_saturation.empty:
            saturation['memory'] = {
                'day': memory_saturation.iloc[0]['days'],
                'traffic': memory_saturation.iloc[0]['conservative'],
                'value': memory_saturation.iloc[0]['predicted_memory']
            }
        
        response_saturation = forecast[forecast['predicted_response'] > 1000]
        if not response_saturation.empty:
            saturation['response'] = {
                'day': response_saturation.iloc[0]['days'],
                'traffic': response_saturation.iloc[0]['conservative'],
                'value': response_saturation.iloc[0]['predicted_response']
            }
        
        return saturation
    
    def plan_capacity(self, growth_rate_percent=10):
        """Generate capacity plan"""
        # Forecast traffic
        traffic_forecast = self.forecast_traffic(days_ahead=365)
        
        # Predict resource needs
        forecast = self.predict_resource_needs(traffic_forecast)
        
        # Find saturation points
        saturation = self.find_saturation_points(forecast)
        
        # Generate plan
        plan = {
            'current_traffic': self.data['requests_per_second'].iloc[-1],
            'current_cpu': self.data['cpu_usage'].iloc[-1],
            'current_memory': self.data['memory_usage'].iloc[-1],
            'current_response': self.data['response_time_p95'].iloc[-1],
            'saturation_points': saturation,
            'recommendations': []
        }
        
        # Add recommendations
        if 'cpu' in saturation:
            days_to_cpu = (saturation['cpu']['day'] - self.data['days_since_start'].max())
            plan['recommendations'].append({
                'type': 'cpu',
                'action': 'Scale CPU capacity or optimize code',
                'timeframe': f"{days_to_cpu} days",
                'priority': 'high' if days_to_cpu < 30 else 'medium'
            })
        
        if 'memory' in saturation:
            days_to_memory = (saturation['memory']['day'] - self.data['days_since_start'].max())
            plan['recommendations'].append({
                'type': 'memory',
                'action': 'Increase memory or optimize memory usage',
                'timeframe': f"{days_to_memory} days",
                'priority': 'high' if days_to_memory < 30 else 'medium'
            })
        
        if 'response' in saturation:
            days_to_response = (saturation['response']['day'] - self.data['days_since_start'].max())
            plan['recommendations'].append({
                'type': 'response_time',
                'action': 'Optimize slow queries or add caching',
                'timeframe': f"{days_to_response} days",
                'priority': 'high' if days_to_response < 30 else 'medium'
            })
        
        return plan, forecast
    
    def visualize_forecast(self, forecast):
        """Visualize capacity forecast"""
        fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(15, 10))
        
        # Traffic forecast
        axes[0,0].plot(forecast['days'], forecast['conservative'], 'b-', label='Forecast')
        axes[0,0].axhline(y=self.data['requests_per_second'].max(), color='r', linestyle='--', label='Current Peak')
        axes[0,0].set_xlabel('Days')
        axes[0,0].set_ylabel('Requests per Second')
        axes[0,0].set_title('Traffic Forecast')
        axes[0,0].legend()
        axes[0,0].grid(True)
        
        # CPU forecast
        axes[0,1].plot(forecast['days'], forecast['predicted_cpu'], 'g-', label='Predicted CPU')
        axes[0,1].axhline(y=80, color='r', linestyle='--', label='Threshold (80%)')
        axes[0,1].fill_between(forecast['days'], 80, forecast['predicted_cpu'], 
                               where=forecast['predicted_cpu']>80, color='r', alpha=0.3)
        axes[0,1].set_xlabel('Days')
        axes[0,1].set_ylabel('CPU Usage (%)')
        axes[0,1].set_title('CPU Forecast')
        axes[0,1].legend()
        axes[0,1].grid(True)
        
        # Memory forecast
        axes[1,0].plot(forecast['days'], forecast['predicted_memory'], 'purple', label='Predicted Memory')
        axes[1,0].axhline(y=80, color='r', linestyle='--', label='Threshold (80%)')
        axes[1,0].fill_between(forecast['days'], 80, forecast['predicted_memory'],
                               where=forecast['predicted_memory']>80, color='r', alpha=0.3)
        axes[1,0].set_xlabel('Days')
        axes[1,0].set_ylabel('Memory Usage (%)')
        axes[1,0].set_title('Memory Forecast')
        axes[1,0].legend()
        axes[1,0].grid(True)
        
        # Response time forecast
        axes[1,1].plot(forecast['days'], forecast['predicted_response'], 'orange', label='Predicted Response')
        axes[1,1].axhline(y=1000, color='r', linestyle='--', label='SLO (1000ms)')
        axes[1,1].fill_between(forecast['days'], 1000, forecast['predicted_response'],
                               where=forecast['predicted_response']>1000, color='r', alpha=0.3)
        axes[1,1].set_xlabel('Days')
        axes[1,1].set_ylabel('Response Time p95 (ms)')
        axes[1,1].set_title('Response Time Forecast')
        axes[1,1].legend()
        axes[1,1].grid(True)
        
        plt.tight_layout()
        plt.show()

# Example usage
# Load historical data
historical = pd.DataFrame({
    'timestamp': pd.date_range(start='2024-01-01', periods=90, freq='D'),
    'requests_per_second': np.random.normal(1000, 200, 90).cumsum() / 10 + 500,
    'cpu_usage': np.random.normal(50, 10, 90).cumsum() / 10 + 40,
    'memory_usage': np.random.normal(60, 5, 90).cumsum() / 10 + 50,
    'response_time_p95': np.random.normal(300, 50, 90).cumsum() / 10 + 250
})

planner = CapacityPlanner(historical)
plan, forecast = planner.plan_capacity()

print("CAPACITY PLAN")
print("=" * 50)
print(f"Current Traffic: {plan['current_traffic']:.0f} req/s")
print(f"Current CPU: {plan['current_cpu']:.1f}%")
print(f"Current Memory: {plan['current_memory']:.1f}%")
print(f"Current Response Time: {plan['current_response']:.0f} ms")
print("\nSaturation Points:")
for resource, details in plan['saturation_points'].items():
    print(f"  {resource}: Day {details['day']} at {details['traffic']:.0f} req/s")
print("\nRecommendations:")
for rec in plan['recommendations']:
    print(f"  [{rec['priority'].upper()}] {rec['action']} - {rec['timeframe']}")

planner.visualize_forecast(forecast)

content.value: Advanced testing patterns help uncover bottlenecks that basic testing misses. Chaos engineering reveals how systems behave under failure conditions. Capacity planning helps you stay ahead of growth. These techniques, combined with the systematic methodology, comprehensive tooling, and optimization strategies covered throughout this guide, provide a complete toolkit for mastering performance bottleneck identification and resolution.

Performance bottleneck identification is both an art and a science. The science comes from systematic methodology, comprehensive metrics, and proper tooling. The art comes from experience—recognizing patterns, knowing where to look, and developing intuition about system behavior.

**Key Takeaways:**
- Bottlenecks can occur anywhere in the stack—don't assume it's the database
- Metrics without context are misleading; always establish baselines
- Use the right tool for each layer: load testing, APM, profiling, database analysis, network tools
- Follow a systematic methodology: detect → scope → analyze → isolate → validate
- Fix the root cause, not the symptom
- Validate your fix with before/after measurements
- Automate detection and monitoring to catch issues early
- Plan for capacity to stay ahead of growth

**Continuous Improvement:**
Performance optimization is not a one-time project but an ongoing discipline. Integrate performance testing into your CI/CD pipeline. Make performance a feature, not an afterthought. Build a culture where developers consider performance implications of their code. Celebrate performance improvements like any other feature.

**Further Learning:**
- Study system design and architecture patterns
- Deep dive into your specific technology stack's performance characteristics
- Learn about your database's internals
- Explore distributed systems concepts
- Practice with load testing tools on sample applications
- Participate in performance engineering communities
- Read performance engineering books and blogs

Remember: Every millisecond counts. Happy optimizing!

quiz.question: What is the most accurate way to measure user-perceived performance?
quiz.explanation: Percentiles like p95 and p99 accurately show what slow users experience, while averages can hide problems. If p99 is high, 1% of users are having a bad experience.

quiz.question: Your application is slow, but CPU usage is low and memory is normal. Where should you look first?
options: Check for database or network I/O bottlenecks
quiz.explanation: Low CPU with high response time typically indicates waiting for something—database queries, network calls, or disk I/O. The application is not CPU-bound; it's I/O-bound.

quiz.question: What tool would you use to identify the most time-consuming methods in a running Java application?
quiz.explanation: Async-profiler is a low-overhead profiler for Java that can generate CPU and allocation profiles, including flame graphs showing exactly where time is spent.

quiz.question: What SQL query pattern often leads to database bottlenecks?
quiz.explanation: N+1 queries occur when you query for a list of items, then loop through them to query related data individually. This can generate hundreds of small queries instead of one efficient JOIN.

quiz.question: What's the first step in the bottleneck identification methodology?
quiz.explanation: Always start by detecting that a problem exists and scoping its boundaries—what's affected, when it started, who's impacted—before diving into analysis.

quiz.question: Which metric would best indicate a connection pool bottleneck?
quiz.explanation: When connection pool is exhausted, threads queue up waiting for a connection. Monitoring active connections vs. pool size and threads awaiting connection reveals pool bottlenecks.

tutorials.title: 🔐 Security Testing
tutorials.description: Master the complete spectrum of security testing, from foundational principles to advanced adversarial techniques. This guide provides an in-depth exploration of vulnerability assessment, threat modeling, tooling, automation, and reporting, empowering you to build resilient and secure systems.

content.title: Beyond Functionality: The Mindset of a Security Tester
content.explanation:
Security testing is not merely a subset of functional testing; it's a distinct discipline with a unique adversarial mindset. While functional testing asks, 'Does the system do what it's supposed to do?', security testing asks, 'What can the system be tricked into doing that it's NOT supposed to do?'

This fundamental shift in perspective is crucial. A security tester must think like an attacker, anticipating malicious inputs, unexpected workflows, and attempts to bypass controls. The goal is to validate the system's confidentiality, integrity, and availability (the CIA triad) against a motivated adversary.

**Key Differences from Functional Testing:**
- **Intentional Abuse:** Security tests attempt to break the system, cause errors, and access unauthorized data.
- **Negative Testing:** It heavily focuses on what the system should *not* allow.
- **Unpredictability:** Attackers don't follow happy paths; they explore edge cases, boundary conditions, and hidden interfaces.
- **Attribution:** The goal is not just to find a bug, but to assess the business impact of a potential exploit.

**Why This Matters:**
- **Prevent Data Breaches:** Protect sensitive customer and company data.
- **Maintain Trust:** Security failures erode user and stakeholder confidence.
- **Ensure Business Continuity:** Attacks can lead to downtime, financial loss, and legal repercussions.
- **Compliance:** Meet regulatory requirements (GDPR, HIPAA, PCI-DSS).
- **Shift-Left Security:** Integrating security early in the SDLC is far cheaper and more effective than fixing vulnerabilities in production.

items.definition: Ensuring that data is accessible only to authorized users. This is about preventing information disclosure. Breaches of confidentiality include data leaks, exposed APIs, and insecure direct object references (IDOR).

Safeguarding the accuracy and completeness of data and processing methods. It ensures that data has not been tampered with by unauthorized parties. Breaches include SQL injection (altering queries) and man-in-the-middle attacks that modify data in transit.

Ensuring that systems and data are accessible to authorized users when needed. Denial-of-service (DoS) attacks are a direct threat to availability. Other issues like resource exhaustion or misconfigurations can also lead to downtime.

Verifying the identity of a user, process, or device. It answers the question, "Who are you?" Weak authentication includes default credentials, lack of multi-factor authentication (MFA), and predictable password recovery mechanisms.

Determining what an authenticated entity is allowed to do. It answers the question, "What are you allowed to access?" Flaws here lead to privilege escalation, where a user can perform actions beyond their intended role.
Ensuring that an action cannot be denied by the entity that performed it. This relies on audit logs, digital signatures, and secure transaction records. It's crucial for accountability and forensics.

content.value: These six objectives form the foundation of all security testing. A comprehensive test plan will assess each of these areas to provide a holistic view of the system's security posture.

content.caption: The CIA Triad forms the core of information security.
content.alt: Venn diagram showing the interconnectedness of Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability.

content.value: Effective security testing is not a one-time event. It is a continuous process integrated into the software development lifecycle (SDLC).

content.title: 2. Security Testing in Depth: Methodologies and Types
2.1 SAST, DAST, and IAST: A Layered Approach

content.value: No single testing method catches everything. A robust security program combines multiple techniques to cover different attack surfaces and stages of the SDLC.

items.definition:
A white-box testing technique that analyzes source code, bytecode, or binaries *without executing* the application. It's like a spell-checker for your code, identifying potential flaws early in development.

**Pros:** Finds issues early (Shift-Left), precise code location, no running app needed.
**Cons:** Can produce false positives, doesn't find runtime or configuration issues.
**Tools:** SonarQube, Checkmarx, Fortify, Semgrep.

A black-box testing technique that analyzes a *running* application by simulating external attacks. It doesn't have access to the source code and tests the application from the outside in.

**Pros:** Finds runtime and configuration issues, language-agnostic, fewer false positives.
**Cons:** Finds issues later in the cycle, can be slower, may not cover all code paths.
**Tools:** OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite, Acunetix.

An advanced technique that combines elements of SAST and DAST. It instruments the application (like a debugger) and monitors its behavior during functional or automated tests (e.g., running alongside Selenium).

**Pros:** Highly accurate with low false positives, provides detailed code context, works in real-time.
**Cons:** Requires agent installation, can have performance overhead, more complex to set up.
**Tools:** Contrast Security, Seeker, Veracode IAST.

While not a testing tool, RASP is a security technology integrated into an application that can detect and block attacks in real-time. It acts as the final line of defense in production.

**Pros:** Provides real-time protection, deep visibility into attacks.
**Cons:** Can impact performance, must be kept updated. Often used in conjunction with testing, not as a replacement.

content.title: Vulnerability Detection by Method
content.caption: IAST often provides the highest detection rate by combining static and dynamic insights. (Illustrative data based on industry reports).

items.definition: Automated scanning of systems and applications to identify known vulnerabilities, such as unpatched software, weak configurations, and default passwords. It's a broad but shallow form of assessment, ideal for continuous monitoring.

A simulated, authorized cyberattack on a system to evaluate its security. Unlike automated scanning, pen testing is goal-oriented (e.g., "reach the customer database") and performed by skilled security professionals who think creatively to bypass controls.

Focuses specifically on APIs, which are a common attack vector. It checks for broken authentication, excessive data exposure, mass assignment, injection flaws, and improper rate limiting. Tools like Postman, OWASP ZAP, and dedicated API security tools are used.

A manual or automated review of system, network, and application configurations against security best practices and benchmarks (e.g., CIS Benchmarks). It ensures that servers, databases, and cloud environments are hardened against attack.

Testing for platform-specific vulnerabilities (Android, iOS), insecure data storage, weak cryptography, and improper use of mobile APIs. It often involves decompiling the app and analyzing its behavior on an emulator or real device.

Evaluating the security posture of cloud infrastructure (AWS, Azure, GCP). It focuses on identity and access management (IAM), misconfigured storage buckets, network security groups, and compliance with cloud provider best practices.

content.value: Understanding the different types and methodologies of security testing allows you to build a comprehensive strategy. SAST catches issues early, DAST finds runtime flaws, IAST provides deep accuracy, and specialized tests target specific domains like APIs and cloud. Together, they form a layered defense, ensuring vulnerabilities are caught at the most efficient and effective stage of the development lifecycle.

To defend a system, you must understand the attacker's tools and techniques. This section dives deep into the most critical and common web application vulnerabilities, as highlighted by the OWASP Top 10.

items.definition: Failures in access control allow users to act outside of their intended permissions. Examples include viewing or editing someone else's account (IDOR), elevating privileges, or accessing unauthorized functions. This is one of the most prevalent and impactful risks.

Previously known as 'Sensitive Data Exposure', this focuses on failures related to cryptography. This includes transmitting data in clear text (no TLS), using weak or deprecated cryptographic algorithms, storing passwords without strong hashing and salting, and using default or weak keys.

Untrusted data is sent to an interpreter as part of a command or query. The attacker's hostile data can trick the interpreter into executing unintended commands or accessing unauthorized data. The most common example is SQL Injection, but it also includes NoSQL, OS command, and LDAP injection.

A new category focusing on risks related to design and architectural flaws. It emphasizes the need for threat modeling, secure design patterns, and reference architectures *before* code is written. It's about preventing the wrong thing from being built in the first place.

This is the most common issue. It results from insecure default configurations, incomplete or ad-hoc configurations, open cloud storage, verbose error messages containing sensitive information, and unnecessary features being enabled (e.g., unused ports, services, pages).

Using components (libraries, frameworks, other software modules) with known vulnerabilities. If you don't know the versions of all components you use, your software is likely vulnerable. This includes failing to scan for vulnerabilities and not updating or patching components regularly.

Broken authentication allows attackers to compromise passwords, keys, or session tokens. This includes allowing weak passwords, credential stuffing, weak session management, and not implementing multi-factor authentication (MFA).

items.term: A08:2021 – Software and Data Integrity Failures
items.definition: Failures related to software updates, critical data, and CI/CD pipelines without integrity checks. This includes applications that rely on plugins, libraries, or modules from untrusted sources, repositories, or content delivery networks (CDNs). An insecure CI/CD pipeline can introduce the potential for unauthorized access, malicious code, or system compromise.

items.term: A09:2021 – Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
items.definition: Without logging and monitoring, breaches cannot be detected. This category ensures that login attempts, access control failures, and server-side input validation failures are logged with sufficient context to identify suspicious activity. It also includes failing to monitor logs for active attacks.

Occurs when a web application fetches a remote resource without validating the user-supplied URL. An attacker can coerce the application to send a crafted request to an unexpected destination, even when protected by a firewall, VPN, or other network access control list (ACL).
